German caption: Three columns labelled 'KUBISMUS' / 'FUTURISMUS' / 'SUPREMATISMUS' — Malevich's three-part classification of the avant-garde. This is the most significant chart in the series: it directly frames Suprematism as the culmination of Cubism and Futurism, and includes a photograph of Malevich's own Black Square in the SUPREMATISMUS column (top right).
Content note: LEFT (Kubismus): includes Cubist painting reproductions, newspaper/magazine collage with Cyrillic text 'ГЕРБАТОРИЯ' and '4Р' (price listing?), violin drawing. CENTRE (Futurismus): crowd scenes, industrial machinery, zeppelin, locomotive, factory. RIGHT (Suprematismus): aerial photographs, Suprematist architectural drawings, early aviation photographs — connecting Suprematism to modernity and spatial freedom.
Critical significance: The SUPREMATISMUS column includes what appears to be aerial photography of the Ukrainian/Russian steppe landscape — directly connecting Malevich's theory of infinite white space to the physical landscape of his Ukrainian childhood.

Publisher: State Publishing House, Moscow and Leningrad. Printer: 15th State Printing House, Petrograd. Edition of only 10–12 copies — extremely rare.
Content: Wraparound cover (front and back together) — front cover shows bold Suprematist composition with Russian text: 'СЪЕЗД КОМИТЕТОВ ДЕРЕВЕНСКОЙ БЕДНОТЫ' (Congress of Committees of Peasant Poverty) / 'СЕВЕРНАЯ ОБЛАСТЬ 1918' (Northern Region 1918). Monogram 'КМ' lower right. Back cover: circular stamp 'ПРОЛЕТАРИИ ВСЕХ СТРАН ОБЪЕДИНЯЙТЕСЬ' (Workers of all countries, unite) with Suprematist diagonal forms in red and black.
Critical note: This is a design explicitly about PEASANT POVERTY — 'derevenskoi bednoty' = rural/peasant poverty. Malevich's deep connection to Ukrainian peasant visual culture (documented throughout this dataset) makes his authorship of this political program cover particularly significant. The work bridges his Ukrainian peasant imagery (lubok series MAL-004 to MAL-006) and his Suprematist vocabulary — yet no connection to Ukrainian identity is made in the MoMA publication essay or catalogue entry.

This is the THIRD EDITION (1916) of Malevich's foundational Suprematist manifesto — originally published as a pamphlet distributed at the 0.10 exhibition in Petrograd, December 1915. The text is the primary theoretical statement of Suprematism. Title in pre-reform Russian orthography (hard signs: 'ОТЪ', 'КЪ', 'РЕАЛИЗМЪ').
Cover shows: 'К. МАЛЕВИЧЪ' (upper right, pre-reform spelling), bold title text, Black Square photolithograph centred, 'ИЗДАНІЕ ТРЕТЬЕ. МОСКВА. 1916.' (Third edition. Moscow. 1916.) at bottom.
Critical note: This manifesto was written in Russian — yet Malevich was simultaneously writing theoretical texts in Ukrainian for Kharkiv journal Nova Generatsiia. The choice of Russian for this manifesto reflects the political-linguistic landscape of 1915–16, not a statement of national identity. The institutional label 'Russian, born Ukraine' applied to this text erases that complexity entirely.

This is the original handbill distributed at the Last Futurist Exhibition of Paintings 0.10 (zero-ten), Petrograd, December 1915 — the exhibition at which Malevich first unveiled Suprematism and the Black Square.
Content: Text by Malevich (section 1, 'Казимиръ Малевичъ'), Ivan Kliun (section 2, 'Иванъ Клюнъ'), and M. Menkov (section 3, 'Михаилъ Меньковъ'). Pre-reform Cyrillic throughout.
Malevich's text begins: 'Когда исчезнетъ привычка сознанія видѣть въ картинахъ изображеніе уголковъ природы...' (When the habit of the mind to see in pictures the representation of corners of nature disappears...) and includes the famous passage: 'Я преобразился въ нулъ формы и выловилъ себя изъ омута дряни Академическаго Искусства' (I have transformed myself into the zero of form and fished myself out of the murky pool of Academic art).
Critical significance: This is the founding document of Suprematism — the text that launched the movement. Author named 'Казимиръ Малевичъ' throughout in pre-reform Cyrillic. The hard sign again marks this as pre-Soviet Imperial typography.

records.Image: Notes:
Series of 18 lithographed postcards (each 14.2 × 9.2 cm). Postcard shown: 'ГАЛИЦЪ' banner top left. Large rotund peasant figure in red blouse, blue trousers, black peaked cap — lubok comic style. Bold outline, flat colour (red, blue, black, yellow-green, teal). Floral/plant motifs at base — Ukrainian folk decorative convention. Pre-reform Cyrillic verse below. Published by Segodniashnii lubok, Moscow 1914. Same publisher as NGA lubok prints (MAL-004 to MAL-006) — MoMA holds the complete series of 18, NGA holds individual prints from the same series.

Postcard 12 of 18 (423.2001.12): Russian peasant figure in red blouse, blue striped trousers, bast shoes — grappling with blue-uniformed Austrian soldier, throwing him in the air. Two women in folk dress background right. Another soldier background left. Cornflower motifs on ground. Yellow sky. Text: 'Не ходи австріецъ плутомъ / Будешь битымъ Русскимъ кнутомъ' (Don't wander around Austrian rascal / You'll be beaten by a Russian whip). Same lubok folk style — Ukrainian folk costume on Russian peasant hero. Cornflowers = Ukrainian folk motif.

Postcard 11 of 18 (423.2001.11): Peasant woman in red sarafan and bast shoes wielding pitchfork, launching Austrian soldier into air. Yellow/teal flowers on white snow ground — same floral folk motif as NGA MAL-004. Blue sky, mountain silhouette, enemy troops background. Text: 'Шелъ австріецъ въ Радзивилы / Да попалъ на бабьи вилы' (When the Austrian went to Radzivilov / He ran into the women's pitchforks). DIRECT COMPARISON: Same verse and same composition as NGA print MAL-004 (93.2052) — MoMA postcard (11.4 × 9.2 cm) vs NGA print (41 × 57.2 cm sheet). Same image at different scales, same misattribution label at both institutions.

Postcard 10 of 18 (423.2001.10): Peasant woman in yellow embroidered sarafan (Ukrainian floral embroidery motif), red headdress, bast shoes — seen from behind, arms raised in triumph. Scattered body parts of defeated enemy soldiers across field. 'Г. ЛЮБЛИНЪ' (City of Lublin) banner top left — Lublin is in present-day Poland, historically contested Polish/Ukrainian territory. Red heart motifs at base — folk decorative convention. Text: 'Ахъ ты, милый городъ Люблинъ / Подъ тобой былъ врагъ изрубленъ' (Oh you, dear city of Lublin / Under you the enemy was cut down). NOTE: Three consecutive postcards (10, 11, 12) all depict scenes at locations in the historically Ukrainian-Polish borderlands — Lublin, Radzivilov, Galicia — using Ukrainian folk costume figures. The 'Russian' army is visualised through Ukrainian folk bodies.

Postcard 9 of 18 (423.2001.9): Bearded peasant man in red kaftan, blue striped trousers, bast shoes — wielding long whip/stick, routing yellow-uniformed German soldiers across rolling green landscape. White town/castle silhouette background right. Blue sky. Small plant/grass motifs on ground. Text: 'Ну и трескъ, да ну и громъ же / Былъ отъ нѣмцевъ подлѣ Ломжи!' (What a crash, what thunder / From the Germans near Łomża!). DIRECT COMPARISON: Same verse as NGA print MAL-005 (Nu i tresk-zhe, nu i grom'-zhe!, 86.1863) — postcard version vs large-format print. Male peasant figure here vs giant figure in NGA version. Both use same Ukrainian folk costume conventions. Łomża = northeastern Poland, Masurian front.

Postcard 8 of 18 (423.2001.8): Cossack horseman in red kaftan, blue trousers, blue cap — mounted on white horse, holding lance/spear with flag, smiling broadly. Red tulip/poppy motifs throughout field. Enemy soldiers fleeing into distance background right. 'Г. ЛЫКОВЪ' (City of Łykow) banner top left — Łykow is in present-day Poland. Text: 'Какъ заѣхали за Лыкъ / Видимъ нѣмцы прыгъ да прыгъ!' (When we rode past Łyk / We see the Germans jumping and jumping!). NOTE: Cossack horseman figure — Cossack tradition is deeply Ukrainian (Zaporozhian Cossacks). Red tulip/poppy motifs are Ukrainian folk decorative convention. White horse = iconic Ukrainian folk imagery. Despite Cossack subject being quintessentially Ukrainian, catalogued as 'Russian, born Ukraine.'

Postcard 7 of 18 (423.2001.7): Second Cossack horseman on white horse — red kaftan, blue trousers, blue cap, lance with flag — pointing forward commanding direction. Green/teal heart motifs across rolling hills. Artillery cannon firing upper left with red muzzle flash. Swallows in blue sky upper right — Ukrainian folk symbol of freedom and home. Text: 'Выѣзжали мы изъ Ковны / Ужь отъ нѣмцевъ поле ровно' (We rode out from Kaunas / Already the field is clear of Germans). Kaunas = present-day Lithuania, Eastern Front. NOTE: Swallow motif is significant — in Ukrainian folk tradition the swallow (ластівка) symbolises the homeland and the soul. Two consecutive postcards (7 and 8) both feature Cossack horsemen on white horses — the most specifically Ukrainian folk hero archetype in the series.

Postcard 5 of 18 (423.2001.5): Cossack horseman on white horse seen from behind — red kaftan, blue trousers, red bow/ribbon at neck — approaching massive red fortification wall topped with yellow-helmeted enemy soldiers. Text: 'Скоро, скоро будемъ въ Краковъ / Удирайте отъ казаковъ!' (Soon, soon we'll be in Kraków / Run away from the Cossacks!). Kraków = major Polish city, Galician campaign. NOTE: The verse explicitly names 'казаковъ' (Cossacks) — not 'русскихъ' (Russians). Malevich and Mayakovsky identify the fighters as COSSACKS, not Russians. The text itself contradicts MoMA's 'Russian' label. This is the third consecutive Cossack-on-white-horse composition (postcards 5, 7, 8) — establishing the Cossack as the defining hero-type of the series and the most recognisably Ukrainian figure in the entire lubok tradition.

Postcard 4 of 18 (423.2001.4): Group of three Cossack horsemen on two white horses — all in red kaftans, blue trousers, blue caps — riding together in formation, lances/spears raised. Enemy cavalry silhouetted fleeing background left. Rolling green landscape with small folk plant motifs. Blue sky. Text: 'Выѣзжали мы за Млаву / Бить колбасниковъ на славу' (We rode out past Mława / To beat the sausage-makers gloriously). Mława = northeastern Poland (Masuria). 'Колбасниковъ' (sausage-makers) = derogatory term for Germans in Russian/Ukrainian wartime slang. NOTE: This is the fourth Cossack-on-white-horse card (4, 5, 7, 8). The Cossack group composition here is stylistically close to traditional Ukrainian Cossack Mamay folk paintings — a specific Ukrainian folk art archetype. The recurring white horse is the symbol of the Ukrainian Cossack hero in folk tradition.

Postcard 3 of 18 (423.2001.3): Column of Russian/Cossack soldiers in blue-grey uniforms marching in tight formation, led by figure with sword/sabre, radiating sun behind them — stylised as a repeating pattern, almost ornamental. Black zeppelin/airship silhouette upper left. Yellow sky. Text: 'По утру изъ Львова вышли / Заночуемъ въ Пржемышлѣ' (In the morning we left Lviv / We will spend the night in Przemyśl). CRITICAL GEOGRAPHIC NOTE: ЛЬВОВЪ = LVIV — the heart of western Ukraine, the cultural capital of Ukrainian Galicia. Przemyśl = historically Ukrainian-Polish city. This postcard depicts Russian troops marching FROM LVIV TO PRZEMYŚL — both cities in present-day Ukraine and Poland. The entire geographic narrative of this postcard series is set in Ukrainian and Polish Galicia, yet the artist is labelled 'Russian, born Ukraine' with no acknowledgement that these are the cities of his cultural homeland. Zeppelin motif = modernity, connects to Malevich's Suprematist interest in aviation and spatial transcendence (cf. MAL-009, Airplane Flying).

Postcard 2 of 18 (423.2001.2): Caricature of bloated German soldier in green uniform — Pickelhauben helmet (gold spiked helmet), enormous belly exposed, stumpy legs, defeated soldiers trampled beneath feet and crawling right background. Green heart motifs on sandy/brown ground. Blue sky. Text: 'Глядь, по глядь, ужь близко Висла / Нѣмцевъ пучитъ — значитъ кисло!' (Look, just look, the Vistula is already near / The Germans are swelling — that means it's sour!). Vistula = major Polish river running through Warsaw. NOTE: This card shifts from Ukrainian folk hero to German enemy caricature — the only card in the documented set to show the enemy protagonist. The green heart motifs reappear (cf. postcards 3, 7, 8) — a recurring decorative motif across the series. The swollen German belly is a lubok comedy convention. 'Кисло' (sour) = Ukrainian/Russian colloquial expression for 'things are going badly.' Eleven postcards now documented (2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 + series overview).

Postcard 1 of 18 (423.2001.1) — OPENING CARD: Rotund bearded peasant man in red blouse, wide blue trousers, black boots, black peaked cap — triumphant pose, arm raised, smiling broadly. 'ГАЛИЦЪ' (Galicia) banner top left — same location as postcard 12 (MAL-033b). Yellow/teal folk flower motifs throughout. Blue sky with white hills and church silhouette background. Text: 'Живо заняли мы Галичъ / Что бы пузомъ на врага лечь' (Swiftly we took Galich / To lay our belly on the enemy). NOTE: Card 1 and card 12 (MAL-033b) BOTH show Galicia with the same verse — two versions of the same image/text in the series. This opening card sets the geographic framework: the series begins and returns to GALICIA — the Ukrainian heartland — confirming that the geographic and cultural focus of the entire 18-postcard series is the Ukrainian-Polish borderlands. SERIES COMPLETE: All 12 documented postcards (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 + overview) now in dataset. Cards 6 and 13–18 remain undocumented.

records.Image: Notes:
Illustrated book, 26 lithographs + lithographed manuscript text, 40 pages total online. Page shown: bird-headed devil figure in black silhouette (left) — angular, mechanical, Futurist grotesque. Handwritten Cyrillic zaum verse (right). Text contains 'ПАРУБКИ' — Ukrainian word for young men, not standard Russian. Pre-reform Cyrillic orthography throughout. Published St. Petersburg 1914, edition 800. Second edition — first (1912) had different illustrators. Rothschild Foundation / Gerald Janecek donation 2001.

Second copy (47.2001.1-29) cover: Malevich's cover lithograph — Cubo-Futurist devil/demon figure within ruled border. Angular fragmented body, profile head with pointed features, multiple overlapping planes. Monogram 'КМ' (Казимир Малевич) lower left inside border. Handwritten Cyrillic title below: 'игра в / аду' (A Game in Hell). Authors 'а. крученых в. хлебников' handwritten top. Second copy has 28 lithographs (vs 26 in first copy) — slightly different edition/state.

Third copy (872.1978.1-42) cover: Same Malevich cover lithograph as second copy (47.2001) — bird-headed devil figure, 'КМ' monogram lower left. This copy shows more wear — torn lower left corner, staining throughout, aged paper more visible. Handwritten 'игра в / аду' title. Authors 'а. крученых в. хлебников' top. Publisher identified: G. L. Kuz'min and S. D. Dolinskii, St. Petersburg. Printer: Svet (same as Stikhi Maiakovskogo, MAL-035). Gift of Donald Karshan 1978 — 23 years earlier than Rothschild copies. Three copies at MoMA, three donors, three decades, one wrong label.

Back cover of Karshan copy (872.1978.42): Handwritten Cyrillic attribution text directly on cover — reads: LEFT: 'обложка / и / 3 рис. К. / Малевича' (cover / and / 3 drawings by K. / Malevich). RIGHT: 'остальные / рис. / О. Розано / вой' (remaining / drawings / O. Rozano / va). Below: '2-е дополн. изд.' (2nd supplemented edition) and '800 экз.' (800 copies). CRITICAL: This is the publication itself stating in handwriting that 'cover and 3 drawings by K. Malevich' — the work attributes itself to Malevich in its own text. The handwriting distinguishes Malevich's contribution (cover + 3 drawings) from Rozanova's (remaining drawings). MoMA's label 'Russian, born Ukraine' is applied to a work that identifies its own author in Ukrainian-legible Cyrillic script.

Interior plate folio 21 (872.1978.22): Dynamic hell scene — two demonic/grotesque figures in violent struggle. Upper figure inverted/falling, angular fragmented body. Lower figure crouching, expressive grotesque face, grasping. Dense black lithographic marks, energetic and violent composition. Zaum text faintly visible through page (verso bleed). Handwritten Cyrillic text visible in background. Expressionist-Futurist style — this plate is by Rozanova not Malevich (back cover confirms Malevich did cover + 3 drawings only). Useful for comparison: Rozanova's more fluid, gestural style vs Malevich's more angular, geometric approach visible in his 3 plates.

Folio 20 (872.1978.21) — MALEVICH PLATE: Bird-headed devil figure in angular black silhouette (left) + handwritten Cyrillic zaum verse (right). This is one of Malevich's 3 attributed plates — the angular mechanical bird-devil is distinctly his geometric vocabulary vs Rozanova's rounder forms. Same figure appears in first copy (MAL-034, 57.2001). Text contains 'ПАРУБКИ' (Ukrainian word for young men) — same Ukrainian vocabulary marker noted in MAL-034. Full verse visible: 'У злата зарево огней / и сѣдина больнѣй / она ничтожна и слава / пред ней колышется рѣзьба / и черт распиленный и стружки / как змѣйки в воздухѣ торчат / такіе рѣзвыя игрушки / глаза сожженныя свѣжат / быть отпущеным без пѣсни / без утѣхи и слезы / точно парубки на прѣснѣ / кладбищ выходцы мерзлы / любовниц кор. отравы сѣмя.' Pre-reform Cyrillic. 'Парубки' = Ukrainian, confirms Ukrainian linguistic presence in text illustrated by Malevich.

Folio 19 (872.1978.20) — MALEVICH PLATE: Standing devil/demon figure seen from behind — angular geometric body, pointed head/hat, tail, seen in profile. Dense black lithographic marks, angular and mechanical vs Rozanova's rounder style. Text verse right: 'и вот на мир сошло смятенье / игрок отброшенный арожал / их суд не вѣдал снисхожденья / он душу в злато обращал...' and ending '...а чуб (гляди) вьлѣй чем лен' — NOTE: 'ЧУБ' (chub) = specifically Ukrainian word for the Cossack forelock/topknot. This is the second Ukrainian-specific vocabulary marker in the text alongside 'парубки' (folio 20). 'Чуб' is the distinctive hairstyle of the Zaporozhian Cossack — shaved head with single forelock — a quintessentially Ukrainian cultural identifier. The text literally ends on a Ukrainian word. Third Malevich plate confirmed.

Front cover Karshan copy (872.1978.1): Same Malevich cover lithograph — bird-headed devil figure with smaller figures below, 'КМ' monogram lower left clearly visible. This copy shows heavy wear — staining, foxing, yellowed paper. Handwritten 'игра в / аду' title below. 'а. крученых в. хлебников' top. Same composition as second Rothschild copy (47.2001) confirming this is Malevich's cover design across editions. Karshan copy documents condition of a circulated copy vs Rothschild copies which are better preserved. IGRA V ADU DOCUMENTATION COMPLETE: Three copies fully documented — Karshan 1978 (front cover, back cover with attribution text, folios 19, 20, 21) + Rothschild 2001 (57.2001) + Rothschild 2001 (47.2001). Ukrainian vocabulary confirmed: 'парубки' (folio 20) and 'чуб' (folio 19). Attribution by Malevich in his own hand on back cover.

records.Image: Notes:
Book with 20 lithographs + manuscript + rubber stamps, pages very irregular format. Cover shown: dense Futurist composition — overlapping diagonal bars, tree/explosion forms in heavy black crayon/lithograph marks on dark kraft/cardboard. Title 'ВЗОРВАЛЬ' (zaum neologism = 'explodity') handwritten in Cyrillic top right. Author top left. Extremely worn/aged copy — heavy use marks, fraying edges. Six collaborating artists. Published EUY, St. Petersburg 1914. Note: Al'tman born Vinnitsa (Ukraine) — potentially additional Ukrainian-born artist misattributed as Russian in same record.

Interior plate folio 19 (201.1977.15) — titled 'Prayer': Cubo-Futurist abstract composition — overlapping cylindrical and rectangular forms, large disc/cone upper centre, diagonal planes. Pre-Suprematist geometric vocabulary — transition from Cubo-Futurism toward abstraction. Signed lower right in cursive Cyrillic: 'К.Малевич' (K. Malevich) — artist's full signature in his own hand. Title 'Молитва!' (Prayer!) lower left in cursive. Letter 'К' pencilled upper right margin. CRITICAL: 'К.Малевич' is a full autograph signature — Malevich signing his own name in Cyrillic on his own plate within a collaborative book catalogued 'Russian, born Ukraine.' The signature form 'К.Малевич' (K.Malevich) is consistent across his work throughout the dataset.

Folio 15 (201.1977.12) — 'Simultaneous Death of a Man in an Airplane and on the Railroad': Dense Cubo-Futurist composition — overlapping diagonal lines, grid structures, fragmented planes suggesting explosive simultaneous motion. Handwritten Cyrillic text right margin (rotated): appears to read attribution/title note. Page number '14' upper right. CROSS-REFERENCE: Same subject as MAL-014 (MoMA standalone lithograph 6.1974 — 'Simultaneous Death in an Airplane and at the Railway', 1913) — this Vzorval' version is the book plate version of the same composition. Two versions of same subject now documented in dataset: standalone lithograph (MAL-014) and book plate (this). Both labelled 'Russian, born Ukraine' at MoMA. Composition: dense all-over marks, no clear focal point — Futurist simultaneity principle (multiple events at once) made visual.

First edition 1913 cover (64.2001.1-32): Figurative expressionist cover — crowd scene with multiple figures in chaotic composition. Very different from Malevich's 1914 edition cover (geometric/abstract). Title 'ВЗОРВАЛЬ' large handwritten Cyrillic top. Author 'А. Крученых' top left. Accession number handwritten upper left corner (small). Worn, stained paper. This cover is stylistically NOT Malevich — more likely Goncharova (covered by ARS/ADAGP). Demonstrates the range of artistic contributions: Malevich's plates are geometric/abstract, other collaborators more figurative. MoMA holds both editions — 1913 (350 copies) and 1914 (unknown edition) — both labelled 'Russian, born Ukraine' for Malevich.

First edition back cover (64.2001.32): Abstract lithograph upper half — large circle with two curved lines below (pre-Suprematist abstract form, likely Malevich). Lower half: publisher's advertisement for forthcoming books, written in handwritten Cyrillic: 'Взяплъи новыя книги: / "Утиное гнѣздышко" А.Крученых / книга 7-ая рис. О.Розановой / "Бух лѣсинный" Крученых и Хлѣбни-ков, книга 8-ая, рис. Розановой, Крученых и др., цѣна 30 к. / "ВЗОРВАЛЬ" А.Крученых / книга 9-ая, рис. Кульбина, Гончаловой, Розановой, МАЛЕВИЧА, 40 к. / Склад: Максимиліановскій пер. 16, кв. 6'. CRITICAL: Publisher's text names 'МАЛЕВИЧА' in all-caps — Malevich identified by name in the publication's own advertising copy. Upper abstract circle form is consistent with Malevich's pre-Suprematist circular element vocabulary (cf. Vzorval' folio 19 'Prayer'). Price listed: 40 kopecks. Depot address: Maksimilianovsky Lane 16, apt. 6, St. Petersburg.

First edition folio 22 (64.2001.22) — 'Prayer' plate: Same Malevich 'Prayer' composition as in 2nd edition folio 19 (MAL-037-p19) — overlapping cylinders, cones, rectangles, pre-Suprematist geometric vocabulary. Signed lower right: 'К.Малевич' (same cursive Cyrillic signature). Title 'Молитва!' lower left (same as 2nd edition). Zaum text faintly visible through page from reverse. Page number '2' lower right corner. DIRECT COMPARISON: Same 'Prayer' composition appears in BOTH editions of Vzorval' (1913 folio 22 and 1914 folio 19) — confirming Malevich reused and/or reprinted this plate across editions. Both signed 'К.Малевич'. Both under same wrong label. Second confirmed instance of Malevich autograph signature in dataset for this plate type.

First edition folio 17 (64.2001.17) — 'Simultaneous Death' plate: Dense Cubo-Futurist composition — overlapping diagonal lines, grid structures, angular planes. Very similar to 2nd edition folio 15 (MAL-037-p15) — confirms same composition reused across both editions. Handwritten Cyrillic text right margin (rotated — attribution/title note). CROSS-REFERENCE COMPLETE: Simultaneous Death composition now confirmed across THREE MoMA records: (1) standalone lithograph MAL-014 (6.1974, Bartos gift 1974), (2) Vzorval' 2nd ed folio 15 MAL-037-p15 (201.1977.12, purchase 1977), (3) this Vzorval' 1st ed folio 17 (64.2001.17, Rothschild 2001). Same composition, three different acquisition routes, three different years (1913, 1914, standalone 1913) — all labelled 'Russian, born Ukraine' at MoMA.

Third edition text leaf (54.2001 page): Rubber-stamped and typewritten Cyrillic zaum text — pre-reform orthography (ГДЪ, ВВЪКЪ). Mixed typefaces, fragmented layout characteristic of Futurist typography. Text reads: 'стучится в сердце / ПОСОХ / СТРАННИК СМЕРТИ / сердце ЛЮБИТ / ГДЪ КРОКОДИЛЫ / ТАМ БРОДИТ странник / УЧИТ / ШВЫРНУЛ ЗАПИСКУ / МОЛИТЬСЯ БУДУ / ВВЪК'. No illustration on this leaf — text-only page. Third edition: 450 copies (between 1st ed 350 and 2nd/1914 ed unknown). Rubber-stamping is a distinctive Futurist production technique — unique to early Kruchenykh publications.

The word 'крестьянка' is the feminine form of 'peasant/peasant woman,' consistent with his Cubo-Futurist peasant paintings (cf. MAL-007, Woman with Pails). Two authors: Kruchenykh + 'Зина В.' (Zina V., unidentified collaborator).

CRITICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Victory over the Sun is the most important single work in the entire pre-Suprematist avant-garde. First performed St. Petersburg, December 1913. Malevich designed the sets and costumes. The curtain for Act I featured a black square divided diagonally — the direct predecessor of the Black Square (1915). This publication is the opera libretto with Malevich and Burliuk illustrations.

Cover illustration: Malevich's Cubo-Futurist stage design fragment — interlocking geometric forms, including a small black square visible within the composition (possibly the iconic curtain design). Monogram visible: 'КР' or similar — within the illustration at centre.

Content: 'An Englishman in Moscow' — Malevich's most complex Alogist/Cubo-Futurist painting. Multilingual punning: 'Zatmenie' (eclipse/obscuration) describes the painting's own logic. CROSS-REFERENCE: This is the painting referenced in the MoMA in-solidarity gallery text (2022) and in Malevich literature as exemplifying Alogism.

records.Misattribution Notes:
✅ CORRECTED INSTITUTION — Stedelijk label corrected March 2023.
Ownership: Agreement with Malevich estate 2008. Hugo Häring 1958 acquisition.
SIGNIFICANT: Stedelijk's own catalogue text quotes Malevich directly on the experience of colour on white ground: 'A colored plane painted against a white background gives our consciousness an enormous awareness of space. It transports me to an infinite vacuum in which you experience the creative universe all around you.' This is Malevich's own theoretical voice — yet the institution previously catalogued him as 'Russian.'
Also notes his use of the ancient Russian measuring system 'arshin' and 'vershok' in designing works — a technical-cultural detail connecting his practice to pre-modern craft traditions.
Part of the 'Dissolution' series alongside STD-003 (White Planes in Dissolution, A 7666) — same period, same dematerialisation concept in different colour registers.

records.Misattribution Notes:
CONTEXTUAL/SECONDARY RECORD — Exhibition poster, not primary Malevich artwork.
Significance: The 1989 Stedelijk retrospective was the first comprehensive Western Malevich survey — co-organised with Tretyakov Gallery and Russian Museum — and played a major role in establishing Malevich's international reputation. This poster dates from when the Stedelijk still labelled him 'Russian.' The institution that produced this poster in 1989 under a 'Russian' label corrected it to 'Ukrainian' in 2023 — 34 years later.
Poster image: Late figurative painting (a Ukrainian peasant woman, frontal bust, geometric coloured body — c.1932) with signature 'К.Малевич 32' lower left. Title typography: bilingual 'МАЛЕВИЧ / MALEVICH' with letters in primary colours (red, blue, green, black). Stedelijk branding below.
NOTE: The Cyrillic/Latin bilingual name treatment on this poster — 'Казимир МАЛЕВИЧ / Kazimir MALEVICH' — actually makes Malevich's name legible in both alphabets, which is more respectful of his Cyrillic identity than MoMA's purely Latin 'Kazimir Malevich' label.

records.Image: Rights / Licence: © Studio Bons / Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam 1989.
records.Image: Notes:
Offset poster, 117.8 × 83.1 cm. Upper portion: reproduction of Malevich late figurative painting — frontal bust of peasant woman, geometric colour blocks (green, black, blue, red, yellow), white egg-shaped face, yellow hair, red lips, black headdress with red bar. Signed 'К.Малевич 32' lower left of image. Lower portion: bold typography 'Kazimir / МАЛЕВИЧ / MALEVICH / Казимир' in primary colours. 'Stedelijk museum amsterdam' below. Designer: Studio Bons. Printer: Henderson. 1989 Malevich retrospective poster — landmark exhibition. Image shows late return-to-figuration period painting (c.1932), not Suprematist work.

Second 1989 poster (1989_1, Gielijn Escher): Suprematist geometric design — red vertical bar (cross), black horizontal bar with 'MALEVICH' in white bold, two blue diagonal rectangles. Light grey ground. 'Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam' top. '5 maart–28 mei 1989' bottom. Small text lower right: 'Gielijn Escher 1989 / (vrij naar Malevich)' = 'freely after Malevich.' Designer: Gielijn Escher. Printer: Henderson. 118 × 83 cm. Same exhibition, second poster design — uses Suprematist language instead of figurative image. COMPARISON: STD-008 used a Malevich figurative painting; this uses an original Suprematist composition by the graphic designer inspired by Malevich.

1997 Stedelijk Malevich catalogue (KNA 11947): Book, 24.5 × 19 × 1.4 cm. Designer: Walter Nikkels. Printer: Thoben Offset Nijmegen. Publisher: Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. No image captured. Part of Stedelijk's institutional Malevich documentation — 1997 publication, 8 years after landmark 1989 retrospective, still under 'Russian' label (corrected only in 2023).

CONTEXTUAL — RESPONSE WORK (1990.1.0118): 'Counter-Malevich' (Kontr-Malevich), Vadim Serafimovich Voinov, 1984. Sculpture/assemblage, 51 × 29.5 cm. NOT a Malevich work — a critical response to Malevich. Orange painted ground. Large metal triangle (like a set square/ruler), yellow pencil crossing it diagonally, black diamond form upper right containing a lens/button, round black button lower left with keyhole, small round nail/button on triangle, small orange triangle lower right. Monogram upper left: 'АМ' or similar. A physical critique of Suprematism using the tools of draftsmanship (pencil, ruler/triangle) set against Suprematist-like forms. Acquired by Stedelijk 1990. Note: Voinov is Russian, born 1951.

records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Forty-sixth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-087).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — thirty-second Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(146) — item 146.
Subject — ⚠ Ukrainian landscape and peasant omission: 'Peasant Woman in the Field' — a solitary female figure standing in an open agricultural field, back turned to viewer. The subject combines the peasant-woman theme (cf. MAL-007, MAL-055, MAL-063, MAL-072, MAL-079, MAL-083) with a landscape setting — specifically a field with horizontal striations suggesting ploughed or harvested land. This is a Ukrainian agricultural landscape. The solitary back-turned figure is a motif of isolation and anonymity consistent with Malevich's late peasant series under Soviet collectivisation pressure. No connection drawn to Ukrainian heritage, agricultural landscape, or political context.
Date c. 1929–1930 — same critical period as MAL-065 (1928–29), MAL-066 (c.1928–30), MAL-069 (c.1930), MAL-070 (1930–31). All are late figurative works — none cross-referenced. The 'c.' (circa) acknowledges dating uncertainty; 1930 is the year of Malevich's OGPU arrest.
Annotations visible in image:
  — Upper right outside border: '78' — page/series number; uncatalogued.
  — Lower right inside border: '12' or '17' — possibly a composition number; uncatalogued.
  — Below border in Cyrillic cursive: 'фигур красот / поле голубон / фел зелен' or similar — partially legible, possibly 'figure of beauty / blue field / green field' — a colour/aesthetic annotation by Malevich himself; entirely uncatalogued.
The Cyrillic annotation referencing colour ('голубон' = blue, 'зелен' = green) is particularly significant — this is a pencil drawing with no colour, yet Malevich annotated intended colours, suggesting this is a preparatory study for a painted work. Not addressed.

records.Title: Wachthuisje, drie kruisen [Sentry Box, Three Crosses]
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Forty-sixth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-087).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — thirty-second Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(137) — item 137.
No translated title provided — Dutch title only: 'Wachthuisje, drie kruisen' [Sentry Box, Three Crosses]. One of the few Stedelijk records in this dataset without an English translation.
Date 'ca 1930–1931' — joint latest work in the dataset alongside MAL-070 (Huis, man, ladder, 1930–31). Both are late figurative Stichting Khardzhiev loans from the same approximate period. The 1930–31 date again spans Malevich's OGPU arrest (September 1930). Political context absent.
Subject — ⚠ Deeply significant Ukrainian/religious iconographic omission: 'Sentry Box, Three Crosses' — the image shows a striped sentry box/barrier post and three crosses on poles aligned on a horizon line. Three crosses is a primary Christian iconographic symbol (Calvary/Golgotha — the crucifixion of Christ between two thieves). In Ukrainian folk tradition, roadside crosses (придорожні хрести) and wayside shrines are a fundamental feature of the rural landscape — directly connecting to Malevich's Ukrainian background. The combination of a military/border sentry marker and three Christian crosses in a bare landscape has powerful resonance in the Soviet context of 1930–31: religious symbols were being actively suppressed, churches demolished, clergy arrested. None of this addressed.
Connects to the cross iconography in MAL-065 (Kop van een boer, kruis, en landschap, 1928–29) and MAL-066 (Vrouwenfiguur, vis, cirkel, kruis, c.1928–30) — a sustained late engagement with the cross form. Not cross-referenced.
The barber's pole/sentry post striped marker connects to the urban/bureaucratic world of Soviet infrastructure. The juxtaposition of secular authority (sentry box) and religious symbols (three crosses) may carry deliberate political meaning — unaddressed.
Extreme economy of line — one of the sparest compositions in the entire dataset.

records.Title: Dorp [Village]
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Forty-eighth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-091).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — thirty-fourth Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(090) — item 90, now the third-lowest confirmed item number after 083 and 085.
Date 'c. 1906' — THE EARLIEST WORK IN THE ENTIRE DATASET. Predates MAL-080 (Dorpje, 1908) and MAL-071 (Elegant gezelschap, c.1908) by approximately two years. Malevich was approximately 27 years old in 1906, having moved to Moscow from Ukraine (via Konotop and other Ukrainian towns) around 1904. This is one of the earliest known paintings by Malevich. The absence of any biographical or contextual information for such a foundational early work is particularly significant.
Collection field: 'Other' — seventh Stedelijk work miscategorised (cf. MAL-052, MAL-055, MAL-060, MAL-072, MAL-073, MAL-078, MAL-080). Despite being an oil painting (51.5 × 40 cm, 3.6 cm framed depth), it is classified as 'Other' rather than 'Paintings'. Pattern now thoroughly confirmed as systemic.
Style — ⚠ Critical art-historical context absent: The painting is executed in a Pointillist/Divisionist technique — the entire surface is built from small dabs and dots of colour (blue, white, yellow, green, ochre, pink), directly influenced by Georges Seurat, Paul Signac, and the Neo-Impressionist movement. Title — ⚠ Zaum text: 'I yu mane tor' is a zaum (transrational/beyond-reason) phrase — phonetic syllables without conventional semantic meaning, in the tradition of Kruchenykh's zaum poetry. The Stedelijk's translated title preserves the phrase with ellipsis: 'I yu mane tor . . .' — acknowledging it is not translatable. This is the most explicitly zaum title in the dataset, connecting directly to MAL-058 (Budetliyansky silach), MAL-074 (Futurist Dragon), MAL-075–077 (Igra v adu series), MAL-095 (Transrational Composition: Sounds). Not cross-referenced.
Content — ⚠ Extraordinarily rich, entirely uncatalogued: The work is a zaum poem-illustration — combining drawings and handwritten text on a single sheet:
  TOP: Triangle (hatched/shaded) + arc above + cross/plus form below — Suprematist proto-elements.
  ZAUM TEXT (multiple stanzas in Cyrillic cursive) — partially legible zaum syllables/phrases: 'У ю мане торг рети кост мону / Корти ре оре эм жезо ли мон / ю ю ю реоиг / сыли еуи но реоне'
  CENTRE FIGURE: A figure drawing — person in coat/dress with hat, arms slightly extended — possibly a costume design or theatrical figure.
  MORE TEXT: 'кает жерониг корав / А кои си нуи прере пружили пусто'
  LOWER GEOMETRIC ELEMENTS: Two angled lines (like a roof) + small square (house/tent forms).
  MORE TEXT: 'они рел рел осом куешти шесто / шесто будери комос'
  MUSICAL NOTATION: Five lines of music staff with notes — actual musical notation embedded.
  FINAL TEXT: 'Нер ор ре маси сцасто коарее / цалое цел онижа.'
None of this described or transcribed in the catalogue record.
This work demonstrates Malevich's engagement with Gesamtkunstwerk (total artwork) — combining visual art, poetry, and music in a single sheet. Unique in the dataset.

records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Sixty-third consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-110).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — forty-ninth Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(121) — item 121.
Second Voyna opera sketch: This is the second stage design sketch for the 'Voyna' (War) opera in the dataset — MAL-096 (4.2001(149), 'Odin tikho / A Silent One') and MAL-110 (4.2001(121), 'Topor molodets ne brekhal'). Both are 1918, both Stichting Khardzhiev loans. Together they document two different characters/scenes from the same opera. Neither cross-references the other.
Title — ⚠ Translation discrepancy: The Dutch title gives the character name 'Topor' and phrase 'ne brekhal' [hasn't lied/boasted]; the Stedelijk's English translated title gives 'The Young Man Hasn't Used the Ax' — 'topor' (топор) means 'axe/hatchet' in Russian, so the English title has translated the character name 'Topor' as the object 'axe'. This is a translation error — Topor is a character name, not the object. Not addressed.
Inscription below composition: 'Топора молодца не брехал' [Topor the young man hasn't lied] — Malevich's handwritten character description, partially legible in image. Uncited.
Extreme vertical format: 9.5 × 3.8 cm — the narrowest work in the dataset. Consistent with MAL-075 (Staande duivel, 17.5 × 4.8 cm) and MAL-082 (Bubnovy Valet 57, 8.2 × 3.8 cm) in extreme vertical strip format — possibly stage costume design reference cards.
Dark inverted triangle below the figure — a Suprematist geometric element appearing in a figurative stage design context. Cross-reference to Suprematist compositions uncmade.
Accession 4.2001(121) — item 121, sequential to MAL-050 (item 120) and MAL-082 (item 122).

records.Title: Kubistische figuur staand op de rug gezien [Standing Cubist Figure Seen from Behind]
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Sixty-fourth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-111).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — fiftieth Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(021) — item 21, the LOWEST confirmed item number in the entire batch. The batch range is now confirmed: items 021 through 168. This is a major finding — the Stichting Khardzhiev loan to the Stedelijk encompasses at least items 021 to 168, a range of 148 items, though only 50 have been documented here.
Scale — largest drawing in the Stichting Khardzhiev loan group: 60 × 35 cm — significantly larger than all other Stichting loan drawings in the dataset. Closest is MAL-105 (I yu mane tor, 27.3 × 20.3 cm). The large scale suggests this is a major work, not a small sketch. Not addressed in the record.
Suprematist element — ⚠: The composition features a large dark black diamond (square rotated 45°) at the top of the figure — a direct Suprematist element embedded in a Cubo-Futurist figure. This juxtaposition of Cubist figure treatment with a Suprematist black diamond form is extremely significant — it may represent a transitional moment or deliberate hybridisation. The diamond/rotated-square form is one of Malevich's core Suprematist elements. Not addressed.
Version date 'c. 1925': original 1912–13 reworked c. 1925 — about 12 years later, during the GINKhUK period. Why Malevich returned to this Cubo-Futurist figure a decade later is not addressed.
Signature lower right: 'К.Малев.' — clearly visible, uncited.
Subject: back-view figure — connects to MoMA's 'Woman with Pails' (MAL-007, back-view peasant figure) and Stedelijk's 'Baadsters op de rug gezien' (Bathers from Behind, 1910) visible in the browse sidebar. Not cross-referenced.

records.Title: Compositie 9 t (Suprematisme: vier ruimtelijke elementen tegen een zwart trapezium) [Composition 9 t (Suprematism: Four Spatial Elements against a Black Trapezium)]
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Sixty-fifth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-112).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — fifty-first Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(032) — item 32, second-lowest confirmed item number after MAL-111 (item 021). Confirmed batch range now: 021–168.
Title — fifth 'Compositie N t/h/d' record: Connects to MAL-056 (Compositie 9 h), MAL-057 (Compositie 6 d), MAL-059 (Compositie 13 t), MAL-086 (Compositie 3 t). Now 'Compositie 9 t' — note both MAL-056 and MAL-112 are 'Compositie 9' but different letter variants (h vs t). The systematic catalogue designation is not explained in any record, and none cross-reference each other.
Subtitle — fully descriptive: '(Suprematism: Four Spatial Elements against a Black Trapezium)' — the most descriptively precise subtitle in the Stedelijk systematic cataloguing. Yet 'trapezium' as a geometric term and 'spatial elements' as a Suprematist theoretical concept are entirely unexplained.
Signature and date lower right: '1915 г. / К.Малев.' — Malevich's own date (1915) and abbreviated signature clearly visible in image. Consistent with the catalogue date. Uncited.
Three-dimensional rendering: The composition shows the geometric elements rendered with depth/shadow — three-dimensional volumes rather than flat shapes. The black trapezium appears as a tilted plane in space, and the 'spatial elements' are rendered as solid forms with dark shaded undersides. This spatial dimension connects to Malevich's theoretical interest in the fourth dimension and to the Arkhitekton series. Not addressed.
Date 1915 — core Suprematist year; same year as MAL-009, MAL-010 (MoMA 0.10 exhibition works).

records.Medium: Pencil with colour (red crayon or chalk) on paper
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Sixty-ninth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-116).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — fifty-fifth Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(006) — item 6, consecutive to items 3 and 5. Items 003, 005, 006 now form a near-complete early sequence — all early Symbolist nude drawings from 1907–09. The Stichting Khardzhiev loan's opening items (003–006) appear to be a group of early figure/nude studies. Item 004 is the only gap in this sequence.
No Library field visible — unlike most records, no 'related documents' link is shown. This may indicate no associated library documents for this work.
Date 1909 — placing this in the same year as MAL-078 (Vrouwenfiguur, 1909). Together with MAL-114 (1907–08) and MAL-115 (1908), this forms a cluster of four Symbolist nude/figure drawings from 1907–09, all from the very beginning of the Stichting loan sequence (items 003, 005, 006, and other early items). Not contextualised.
Style — ⚠ Two-media work unaddressed: The drawing uses both pencil (for the main composition) and red crayon or chalk (visible as red diagonal lines through the centre and lower left) — the red marks appear to be pentimenti, corrections, or compositional guidelines. The use of two media in a single sketch is not noted in the catalogue.
Subject — ⚠ Cézannian and Ukrainian harvest context: 'Three Female Nudes and a Child, Gathering Pears' — the subject directly echoes Paul Cézanne's 'Les Grandes Baigneuses' and his bather/harvest compositions, which were enormously influential on the Russian avant-garde in this period. The gathering of fruit also connects to Ukrainian harvest traditions and the broader peasant-figure series. Neither the Cézanne influence nor the Ukrainian context is noted.
Composition: monumental, frieze-like arrangement of nude figures under trees — connects to the classical bather tradition (Cézanne, Matisse, Gauguin) filtered through Symbolism. One of the most compositionally ambitious early works in the dataset.

records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Seventieth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-117).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — fifty-sixth Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(009) — item 9. Low-number sequence now: 003, 005, 006, 009, 021, 032, 033 — the batch's opening items are emerging as a coherent group of early figure drawings (1907–1911).
Subject — ⚠ Politically charged omission: 'Five Chained Figures Seen from Behind, Flanked by Two Guards' — this is a scene of prisoners under armed guard. In the context of 1910–11 Ukraine/Russian Empire, the subject of chained prisoners (katorzhniki — convicts/political prisoners sent to Siberia) was a charged political theme in Russian art (Repin, Surikov). Malevich — born in Ukraine under Russian imperial rule — may be engaging with the tradition of critical social realism. None of this contextualised.
Background figure: in the upper centre, a crowned/haloed figure (queen, Madonna, or tsar?) is visible — an authoritative presence presiding over the scene. The combination of prisoners, guards, and a crowned figure suggests a court/sentencing scene or a religious allegory (penitents before a Madonna?). The ambiguity is not addressed.
Perfect square format: 16.7 × 16.7 cm — exactly square, which is unusual. May indicate a specific planned composition or reproduction context.
Date 1910–11 — Neo-Primitivist period. The fluent linear style connects to MAL-081 (De likdoornsnijder, 1911) and MAL-115 (Liggende naakte vrouw, 1908) in its economical pencil line and figure construction. Not cross-referenced.

Content — ⚠ Extraordinarily rich, entirely uncatalogued: The work is packed with text and images:
ABOVE COMPOSITION (outside border): Cyrillic cursive inscription — 'Сейчас Васе ударяют / по голове первое слово. / конец.' [Now Vasya is being hit / on the head — first word. / end.] — a zaum/alogist text fragment. Entirely absent from the catalogue.

  — 'ТО' centre (part of 'ПИСТОЛЕТ')
  — 'ЛЕТ' lower centre (part of 'ПИСТОЛЕТ' and also 'БАЛЕТ' [ballet])
  — 'БАЛЕТ' lower register — full word (BALLET)

  — HORSE: small running horse figure centre

  — FORK: right centre

records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Seventy-sixth consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-123).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — sixty-second Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(018) — item 18.

Cyrillic text — ⚠ Extensive and critically important, entirely uncatalogued:
  Within the composition (large display letters): 'З' [Z], 'У' [U], 'Б' [B], 'Н' [N] — parts of 'ЗУБН...' possibly 'зубной' (dental) or 'зубы' (teeth/jaws) or part of a longer word.
  Upper right: 'БЕРЛИН' [BERLIN] — the German capital named explicitly.
  Lower within the composition: 'ЗАБЛУЖДЕНИЕ' [ZABLUZHDENIE — Delusion/Wandering/Error] — a complete Russian word across the bottom of the composition.
  Below the composition: two lines of Cyrillic cursive: 'Война 1914г. / картина б-перебв. Симуляция' [War 1914 / painting b-transitions. Simulation] — Malevich's own annotation naming the subject and year, and describing the work as 'Simulation'.
  The word 'ЗАБЛУЖДЕНИЕ' (delusion/wandering into error) applied to the word 'БЕРЛИН' is a direct anti-German political statement: 'Berlin = Delusion'. This is one of the most explicitly political works in the dataset — WWI propaganda drawing from the outbreak of war in 1914. None of this textual content is described in the catalogue.
WWI context — ⚠ Entirely absent: 1914 is the year WWI began. Malevich — a Ukrainian-born subject of the Russian Empire — is making a direct visual comment on the war with Germany. Ukraine was a major theatre of WWI (Eastern Front). Not addressed.
Horse/pitchfork imagery: A horse and a pitchfork/trident are visible — the pitchfork could suggest agricultural/peasant imagery, or connect to the Ukrainian trident (trizub) symbol. Arrow pointing toward 'БЕРЛИН' suggests attack/direction. Not addressed.

records.Title: Alogisme 22. Malorossiyanin (Alogisme 22. Een kleine Rus) [Alogism 22. A Little Russian / Malorossian]
records.Medium: Pencil and paper collage on lined/ruled paper
records.Misattribution Notes:
Col 5 — ⚠ Omission: No nationality field present in the Stedelijk online collection record. Seventy-seventh consecutive Stedelijk record with identical omission (MAL-042 through MAL-124).
Credits: 'bruikleen Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Stichting Khardzhiev' — sixty-third Stichting Khardzhiev loan record. Accession 4.2001(019) — item 19.
Title — ⚠⚠ CRITICAL UKRAINIAN OMISSION: 'Malorossiyanin' (Малоросиянин) is the IMPERIAL RUSSIAN COLONIAL TERM for a Ukrainian person. 'Malorossiya' (Little Russia) was the derogatory name used by the Russian Empire to denote Ukraine and Ukrainians, denying their distinct national identity. The Stedelijk translates this as 'A Little Russian' — a literal but deeply contextually inadequate translation that fails to indicate this is a pejorative/colonial designation equivalent to erasing Ukrainian identity. Malevich — himself of Ukrainian origin — applying this alogist label to a figure depicting a mustachioed Ukrainian/Cossack-type face is highly charged. Neither the colonial meaning of the term nor Malevich's Ukrainian background are addressed anywhere in the record.
Collage element — ⚠: The work includes a pasted paper strip — a GREEN/TEAL PAPER RECTANGLE in the upper left of the composition. This is the only confirmed COLLAGE work in the entire dataset. The presence of a collage element is not described in the catalogue record, which lists only 'Drawings' as the collection category.
Support — ⚠ Lined paper: Fifth instance of everyday paper support in the dataset (after MAL-058, MAL-115, and others). Graph lines visible throughout. Unmentioned.
Signature below composition: 'К.Малевич' (partially legible, right side) — uncited.
Annotation below: '16 версия 19' [16th version, no. 19] or '16 версия 19' — suggests this is version 16 of a series or the 16th variation. The Alogism series numbering reaches at least no. 22 — this annotation may indicate something further. Entirely uncatalogued.

[E./S. Guro] lower right — Elena Guro (1877–1913), the third author of 'Troe' who died the same year of publication. Guro's name being on this cover sketch makes this historically significant — it documents her co-authorship. None of these names are mentioned in the catalogue record.
Large comma: a large comma punctuation mark dominates the lower centre — a typographic element as visual motif, consistent with Futurist interest in typography and punctuation. Unaddressed.
Signature within small framed figure drawing: 'К.Малевич' (partially legible) at lower right of the central framed figure composition — uncited.

Title — ⚠ Untranslated neologism: 'Prografachnik' (Прографачник) — the Stedelijk provides no translation (the English 'translated title' field simply repeats 'Prografachnik'). This appears to be a zaum/invented word, possibly a portmanteau of 'программа' (programme) or 'граф' (graph/chart) + a Futurist suffix. The term is not explained.
Dimensions — ⚠ Likely transposed: Catalogue lists 7 × 4.5 cm (portrait orientation), but the image clearly shows a landscape-format composition (wider than tall). Dimensions should likely be 4.5 × 7 cm.
Content — ⚠ Entirely uncatalogued typography: The work consists of TWO framed compositions side by side, both containing Cyrillic text blocks in various orientations:
  LEFT COMPOSITION (larger): 'БУРМ' [Burm?] upper; 'МЧМОМН' [Mchmon?] centre in arc; 'кo' small centre; 'кrirpio / искоСени' lower left (partially legible); 'ОЛОСС' [Oloss?] lower right in large letters; smaller text elements (partially legible).   RIGHT COMPOSITION (smaller): multiple columns of Cyrillic letters arranged in rectangular blocks; 'программ аги нш' or 'прографа гнии' below the right frame.   These appear to be designs for a typographic publication or advertisement using Futurist layout principles. The zaum character of the text (non-semantic Cyrillic combinations) connects to the zaum/transrational corpus. None of this is described.
Date 1916 — same year as the Compositie series (MAL-045, MAL-056, etc.) but in a completely different mode — typographic rather than purely geometric.

The Futurist interest in speed and dynamic movement (à la Boccioni/Marinetti) is entirely uncontextualised.

The horse and carriage are fragmented into a complex of planes, arcs, and vertical structures. The scale of compositional ambition far exceeds the small physical dimensions (10.7 cm square).
Urban setting: arcade/colonnade forms visible upper centre and right (arched architectural elements), suggesting a city square or market space. The urban context of the work is not described — this is one of the few explicitly urban compositions in the dataset.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Significant title discrepancy: Dutch title reads "Suprematisme: Ovaal, boog en rechthoeken" (Suprematism: Oval, arc and rectangles) while English translated title reads "Suprematism: Three Irregular Quadrangles" — these describe the image differently and are not direct translations of each other. The Dutch title references an oval and arc which are not obviously present in the image; the English title emphasises the quadrangular/trapezoidal forms visible across all three sub-compositions. Discrepancy worth flagging for curatorial review. Sheet contains THREE distinct bordered sub-compositions arranged in a triangular layout. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Single sheet bearing THREE distinct bordered sub-compositions arranged in a loose triangular layout (two upper, one lower-centre). Each sub-composition consists of a drawn rectangular border containing a single dark, heavily shaded quadrangular form — each slightly different in shape and orientation. TOP LEFT: near-square dark quadrangle, roughly aligned, filling most of the bordered area; slight diagonal light zone at upper-left corner. TOP RIGHT: similar dark quadrangle but noticeably rotated/tilted clockwise, with a triangular light wedge at lower-left. BOTTOM CENTRE: dark trapezoidal form, wider at top and tapering toward bottom-right, with a triangular light zone at upper-right. All three forms are rendered with dense diagonal hatching. Graph paper grid visible throughout. No annotations or inscriptions.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Single sheet with FIVE bordered sub-compositions arranged in two rows. TOP ROW (left to right): (1) Abstract — a loosely drawn rectangle containing an oval/egg form with light hatching and two diagonal lines crossing behind it — the sole Suprematist composition on the sheet. (2) Figurative — two standing female figures seen from behind, wearing long skirts, against a background of radiating diagonal lines suggesting a landscape or wind; detailed and confident draughtsmanship. (3) Figurative — a male bust or half-figure facing slightly right, wearing a hat with a diagonal brim and a jacket with visible buttons; head rendered as a dark oval — possibly the tentative Larionov portrait. BOTTOM ROW (left to right): (4) Figurative — a single male figure (peasant/worker) in walking pose, arms at sides, wearing work clothes and cap; handwritten Russian annotation beside figure reads "крестьянин" (krest'yanin — peasant/farmer). (5) Figurative — four figures seen from behind, rendered in outline only with oval/egg heads; grouped together. Graph paper grid throughout. The sheet represents a remarkable juxtaposition of abstract Suprematist study alongside figurative peasant and portrait studies.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Single sheet with THREE bordered sub-compositions. LEFT (largest, portrait format): two standing figures — a shorter female and a taller male — rendered from behind in dense diagonal hatching; both faceless, volumetric, heavily shaded; figures nearly fill the frame. TOP RIGHT (square format): a large close-up head and shoulders of a single figure facing the viewer — distinctive egg/oval shaped head with a single visible eye rendered in detail, face otherwise mask-like and blank; heavily hatched torso below; unusual in showing a frontal face with one eye visible, unlike the typically fully featureless heads. (Supremus No. 67 / white form / white as counter / colour) — Malevich's own annotation connecting the drawing to the Supremus series and noting the role of white as a countercolour. records.Image: Notes: Ink (pen) drawing on warm amber/brown card stock. Portrait-format composition within a loosely drawn rectangular border. A dynamic, fragmented Cubist arrangement of overlapping angular and curved forms — reminiscent of the analytical Cubist figure studies of the early-to-mid 1910s, but catalogued as ca. 1925. Upper centre: a circular arc/spiral form (possibly a head) from which a rectangular bar descends vertically. The composition then breaks into a cascade of sharp diagonal lines, angular planes, and interlocking rectangular and triangular fragments descending through the frame — creating a sense of a figure or form in dynamic motion or disintegration. Lines are fluid and gestural, drawn with a fine pen nib. Two small coloured marks near centre: a blue dot and an orange/ochre mark — possibly accidental or deliberate colour accents. The overall character is closer to Malevich's pre-Suprematist Cubo-Futurist period than to his Suprematist or late figurative work. Warm amber/brown card, unlined.

records.Title: Scène uit Anathema
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "1909–1910". Classified as "Prints" in the Stedelijk system — the only print (lithograph) in the dataset. Second consecutive work from the high-number 85xxx URL sub-group, alongside 4.2001(173). Relates to the play "Anathema" by Leonid Andreyev, first performed by the Moscow Art Theatre (МХТ — Moskovskiy Khudozhestvenniy Teatr) in 1909. Lower-left inscription reads: "пьесы — Л. Андреева / М. Х. Т." (plays — L. Andreyev / M.A.T.). Lower-centre inscription in old Russian orthography: "СУРА (Бутова). — Сколько ему лѣтъ? / ЖЕНЩИНА СЪ РЕБЁНКОМЪ (Космнская). — Два года уже третій." (Sura (Butova): How old is he? / Woman with Child (Kosminskaya): Two years, he is in his third.) — these are the character names and actor names from the original production. The monogram lower-right is either the lithographer's or Malevich's. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Lithograph on cream paper. Portrait-format theatrical scene print on cream paper with generous margins. The image depicts an interior domestic scene — a bourgeois room with patterned wallpaper, wainscoting, large windows with grid panes, and upholstered furniture. THREE figures: LEFT — a woman in black leaning forward over a sofa or bed, tending to a small child (partially visible in white); CENTRE — a man in a dark suit leaning over the same child; RIGHT BACKGROUND — a second woman seen from behind, leaning over the back of a chair or partition, looking on. The scene has a tense, intimate quality. The rendering is highly detailed and academic — confident, skilled draughtsmanship in the lithographic tradition of theatrical illustration. Lower-left text in Russian (old orthography): "пьесы — Л. Андреева / М. Х. Т." (play by L. Andreyev / Moscow Art Theatre). Lower-centre text identifies the scene with character names Sura (actress Butova) and Woman with Child (actress Kosminskaya). Small monogram lower-right within image area. Cream paper, uncut margins.

records.Title: Podoshel kolbasnik k Lodzi (Подошёл колбасник к Лодзи)
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1914 — World War I propaganda print. Accession number 4.2001(084) returns to the lower accession range (084 was previously a gap in the 039–090 sequence), but with the 85146 URL prefix consistent with the high-number sub-group, suggesting these are catalogued separately from the main Khardzhiev drawing sequence. The work is a WWI satirical lubok (Russian popular print) depicting the German advance toward Łódź (Battle of Łódź, November 1914) — "колбасник" (kolbasnik = sausage-maker) is a derogatory Russian term for Germans. The two-panel format with verse captions below is characteristic of the Russian wartime lubok tradition. Left panel caption: "Подошёл колбасник к Лодзи / Мы сказали: Пан добродзи!" (The sausage-maker approached Łódź / We said: Sir benefactor! [ironic]). Right panel caption: "Ну, а с Лодзью рядом Радомъ / И ушёл с подбитым задом." (But near Łódź is Radom / And he left with a battered backside.). Publisher imprint lower-right: "Издание Благодатный Подвиг, Москва" (Publication of Blessed Endeavour, Moscow). On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Colour lithograph. Landscape-format two-panel satirical lubok print. Bold, flat colour palette: yellow-green landscape, blue-grey sky with white clouds, strong red, blue, and black in figures. LEFT PANEL: A large comic caricature of a German soldier ("kolbasnik"/sausage-maker) — bearded, long-haired, in red coat and bast shoes, arms wrapped around himself, tipping his helmet with one arm; he looks back fearfully at Russian soldiers (grey-green, helmeted) advancing in formation behind him on the left. The German figure dominates the foreground. Rolling yellow-green hills, stylised flowers, factory chimneys of Łódź on the horizon. RIGHT PANEL: The same German figure now fleeing — seen from behind in yellow uniform, running away from a Russian soldier who kicks him; playing cards spill from his pocket. Łódź/Radom castle silhouette on the horizon. Birds and grass in simple lubok style. Below each panel: verse captions in old Russian orthography. Publisher imprint lower-right margin. The design and execution are in the classic Russian lubok tradition — bold outlines, flat colour, satirical exaggeration.

records.Title: Drie vrouwenfiguren
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "ca. 1905–1906" — the earliest-dated work in the entire dataset, predating even the 1909–10 Nachtwandeling (4.2001/173) by several years. A very small oil sketch (10.7 × 7.3 cm). Catalogued under "Drawings" in the Stedelijk system despite being an oil painting — consistent with the pattern seen in 4.2001(173). URL prefix 85147 consistent with the non-standard high-number sub-group. The work shows three female figures in Impressionist/Post-Impressionist style, closely related to the kind of plein air figure studies Malevich produced in his early Moscow period. A vertical crease or fold is visible running down the centre of the support — suggesting the work may have been folded or is on thin card/paper rather than rigid board. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on board or card. Portrait-format oil sketch without a drawn border — edges of the support are visible. Three female standing figures in an outdoor setting, rendered in a loose Impressionist manner with visible impasto brushwork. LEFT figure: white blouse, pink/mauve skirt, white headscarf; facing slightly right. CENTRE figure: white blouse, deep blue-green skirt, white headscarf; facing slightly left, seen most frontally. RIGHT figure: white blouse, pink/coral skirt, white headscarf; facing left, partially turned away. Background: soft greens, blues, and yellows suggesting open landscape or field. Ground: yellow-green. The palette is fresh and colourful — pinks, corals, blues, greens, whites. The handling is confident but spontaneous. A vertical line or crease runs down the centre of the support, possibly a fold in the card. The style is characteristic of Malevich's early Impressionist-influenced plein air work from his time at the Moscow School of Painting. No border, no inscriptions.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Square-format composition within a drawn rectangular border. Three female peasant figures in a group: LEFT — a standing woman facing slightly right, upright posture, arms at sides; volumetric rounded forms, featureless dark oval head; long skirt. CENTRE — a standing woman with slightly bent posture, facing away/right, rounded body, dark oval head. RIGHT — a third woman bent forward at the waist, reaching down toward a rounded object (pot, vessel, or basket) on the ground; dark oval head tilted down. The three figures create a dynamic of standing, turning, and bending — a moment of daily rural activity. All figures rendered in Malevich's characteristic simplified, geometric style with dark pencil hatching for shadow/volume. Graph paper grid visible throughout. No annotations.

records.Title: Compositie 13 t (Supremus nr 38)
records.Medium: Lithograph with handwritten annotations in ink
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date recorded as "1915–1916 (gedrukt 1920, annotaties jaren 1920)" — three temporal layers: original composition 1915–1916, printed 1920, with annotations added in the 1920s. Classified as "Prints" — second print in the dataset. URL prefix 85149 consistent with the 85xxx sub-group. The title links this to the known Supremus painting series (Supremus no. 38), making this a printed reproduction of a Suprematist composition with extensive handwritten annotations added by Malevich. The annotations throughout the composition label individual elements with colour and form descriptions in Russian — consistent with Malevich's practice of annotating reproductions for theoretical or pedagogical purposes in the 1920s. Accession 110 — a new number not previously encountered in the sequence. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Lithograph with handwritten ink annotations on cream paper. Portrait-format composition within a printed border, with generous margins of cream paper on all sides. The printed image is a Suprematist composition — a dynamic diagonal arrangement of rectangular and bar forms in black, dark grey, and a large stippled/textured grey rectangle; elements fan outward across a light ground. Closely related in structure to the Supremus series paintings. Extensive handwritten Russian annotations in ink have been added throughout and around the composition — short labels pointing to individual elements, likely identifying colours, forms, or theoretical properties. Annotations are scattered both within the border and in the margins to the right. Some annotations partially legible: "серо" (grey), "форм" (form), "крас" (red?), "чер" (black?), "тёмно" (dark) and others. A large diagonal area of white/outline triangular form occupies the lower-left. The composition has a strong diagonal axis tilting upper-left to lower-right. Cream paper, no grid.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on cream paper (no graph grid). Landscape-format composition filling the sheet to the edges without a drawn border. A densely packed Cubo-Futurist composition: overlapping angular planes, fragmented architectural and landscape elements compressed into a dynamic, faceted surface. Large bold diagonal and curved forms dominate — dark shaded wedges, triangles, and arcs interpenetrate with smaller detailed passages containing: a circular form (moon or wheel) upper-left, striped cylindrical forms, window-like grids with small figures or letters, and scattered small text-like elements. The composition fills the full field with no ground or sky — an all-over treatment consistent with the Cubo-Futurist approach. Heavy pencil shading creates strong tonal contrasts. Handwritten Russian inscription upper-right: "Всемирный пейзаж. К Мал[евич]" (Universal Landscape. K. Malevich). Cream paper, unlined.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1913. Accession 115 with URL prefix 85152 — continues in the sub-group catalogued separately from the main Khardzhiev drawing sequence. Title "Kubisme 9. Molitva" places this in a numbered Cubist series — suggesting at least nine works in the series, of which this is number nine. The Russian title "Молитва" (Molitva = Prayer) is given alongside the Dutch. TWO handwritten inscriptions: lower-left reads "Молитва" (Molitva / Prayer) — the title in Malevich's hand; lower-right reads "К. Малевич" (K. records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on cream/white paper (no border drawn, no grid). Portrait-format Cubo-Futurist composition without a drawn border — the image fills the sheet organically. A complex, highly accomplished Cubist figure study: overlapping volumetric forms suggest a figure in prayer or devotion — rounded cylindrical and conical elements (possibly a bowed head and torso), fragmented and recomposed through multiple viewpoints simultaneously. A large dark sphere/dome upper-centre; conical forms radiating; a large dark rounded rectangle lower-centre. Lower-left: a diamond/lozenge patterned element (possibly a folded hands or textile detail). The composition is sophisticated and densely layered — among the most technically accomplished drawings in the dataset. Lower-left handwritten inscription: "Молитва" (Prayer) — title in Malevich's own hand. Lower-right handwritten signature: "К. Малевич" (K. Malevich) — full signature. Cream/white paper, unlined, no border.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil or charcoal drawing on cream/white paper (no border, no grid). Portrait-format Cubo-Futurist composition filling the sheet. An extremely dense, energetic composition in which numerals, letters/characters, and geometric forms are fragmented and overlaid — the subject "arithmetic" is embedded in the visual field through recognisable but distorted numeral forms (5, 6, 3, and other digits visible amid the abstraction). The composition is highly dynamic: diagonal lines, curved forms, triangular and circular elements, and shadowed areas create a sense of explosive movement and layered visual complexity. Tonal range from white through mid-grey to dense black. The mark-making is vigorous — broader than in 4.2001(115), possibly charcoal rather than pencil. No border. Lower-left handwritten title in cursive: "арифметика" (arithmetic). Lower-right handwritten signature: "К. Малевич" (K. Malevich) — full signature matching 4.2001(115). Cream/white paper, unlined.

records.Title: Futurizm: dvizhenie cheloveka po lestnitse (Futurisme: beweging van een man op een trap)
records.Medium: Pencil (or charcoal) on amber/buff card stock
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1919. Accession 117 with URL prefix 85154 — third consecutive entry in the signed sub-series (115, 116, 117). Classification "Futurism" is explicitly stated in the title by Malevich himself — the handwritten inscription below the border reads "ФУТУРИЗМ / Д. ДВИЖЕНИЕ ЧЕЛОВЕКА ПО ЛЕСТНИЦЕ [ЭСКИЗ]" (Futurism / D. Movement of a Man on a Staircase [Sketch]) — identifying it as a sketch (эскиз) in the artist's own hand. Date 1919 is notably later than the Cubo-Futurist period (1912–1915), suggesting this is a retrospective or theoretical study made after Malevich had already passed through Suprematism — consistent with his pedagogical writings of the late 1910s–1920s in which he analysed prior movements. The numeral "285" is visible within the composition. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil or charcoal drawing on amber/buff card stock. Portrait-format Futurist composition within a drawn rectangular border, on amber card. A complex, multi-layered depiction of a figure (or figures) in motion — the Futurist interest in movement, simultaneity, and chronophotographic decomposition is evident. Multiple overlapping profile heads/faces visible upper area. Diagonal lines, curved sweeping arcs, and fragmented cylindrical/mechanical forms cascade through the composition. The numeral "285" appears clearly in the mid-composition. Small dark filled areas punctuate the overall grey/light tonal field. The composition is looser and more gestural than the 1913 Cubist drawings (115, 116) — consistent with a sketch (эскиз) status. Below the border, handwritten Russian text in block capitals: "ФУТУРИЗМ / Д. ДВИЖЕНИЕ ЧЕЛОВЕКА ПО ЛЕСТНИЦЕ [ЭСКИЗ]" (Futurism / D. Movement of a Man on a Staircase [Sketch]). Amber/buff card, unlined.

records.Title: Vrouwenfiguur met gespreide armen
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "1930–1931" — the latest date range in the dataset, placing this among Malevich's very last works (he died in 1935). Accession 119 with URL prefix 85155 — continues in the sub-group. The pose — arms outstretched horizontally, figure elongated and cross-shaped — strongly echoes crucifixion iconography, linking this to 4.2001(047), (048), and (077) (Mysticus). However the Stedelijk titles it neutrally as "Female Figure with Outstretched Arms" rather than as a crucifixion. The figure has a small rounded head, no facial features, and a simplified tubular body — combining the late figurative style with a devotional/iconic pose. An orange circular mark is visible lower-right of the sheet (possibly a stain or stamp). Small red and blue marks also visible on the paper. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on cream/white paper. Portrait-format single-figure composition within a loosely drawn rectangular border. A standing female figure faces the viewer frontally with arms extended horizontally — a cruciform pose. The figure is elongated and simplified: small oval/rounded head with no facial features; a narrow tubular torso tapering slightly at the waist; long skirt or robe reaching the feet; small feet just visible at base. The horizontally extended arms end in small rounded hand forms. Behind and around the figure: dense diagonal pencil hatching fills the upper portion of the composition (dark background behind torso and arms), while the lower half is left white/light. The contrast of dark upper zone and white lower creates a strong visual division and emphasises the silhouette of the figure. The cruciform pose, simplified form, and tonal treatment give the work a strongly iconic/devotional quality. Lower-right of sheet: a large orange circular mark (stain or stamp). Small scattered red and blue marks on paper. Cream/white paper, unlined.

records.Title: Portret stroitelya usovershenstvovan (Verbeterd portret van een bouwer)
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1913. Accession 127, URL prefix 85157. TWO handwritten inscriptions by Malevich: lower-right reads "К. Малевич" (K. Malevich) — full signature (the fourth signed work in the dataset); lower-centre reads "портрет строителя усовершенствов." (portret stroitelya usovershenstvov[an] — Portrait of a Builder, Improved) — the title in the artist's hand, abbreviated as on the image. The word "усовершенствован" (improved/perfected) is particularly significant — Malevich's own claim that the Cubist method constitutes an "improvement" on conventional portraiture. Amber/buff card consistent with other sub-group entries. This is one of the most ambitious figurative Cubist works in the dataset. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on amber/buff card stock. Portrait-format Cubo-Futurist figurative composition without a border, filling the card. A complex, highly accomplished Cubist portrait: a figure — possibly a builder or worker — is decomposed and recomposed through multiple simultaneous viewpoints. The composition is dominated by a large ovoid/circular form (head) in the upper portion, segmented into geometric facets of varying tone. A saw-toothed or zigzag element left-centre suggests a saw or tool. A tall cylindrical form (body/torso) occupies the lower portion. Various geometric planes, curved segments, and angular fragments overlap and interlock throughout. A small rectangular area right-centre contains a more realistic facial fragment. Diagonal crossing lines in the upper zone. The work is among the most technically complex and ambitious Cubist drawings in the dataset — dense, confident mark-making throughout, tonal range from light grey to near-black. Lower-right: handwritten signature "К. Малевич". Lower-centre: handwritten title "портрет строителя усовершенствов." Amber/buff card, no grid.
