records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1915. Accession 139, URL prefix 85163. This work is categorically distinct from all other entries: the "drawing" consists entirely of a drawn rectangular border containing only the handwritten word "Деревня" (Derevnya = Village) in cursive — no pictorial image. Below the border, a multi-line handwritten Russian text in ink (5–6 lines, partially legible). This places the work at the intersection of visual art and text/poetry — consistent with Malevich's Alogist phase (1913–1915) in which he rejected conventional pictorial logic. The catalogued dimensions (5 × 5.9 cm) refer to the drawn border only. Note: "Alogisme 29. Derevnya" also appears in the Stedelijk's alphabetical listing in the "More work from this maker" section in the main 13xxx URL group — it is unclear whether this 85xxx entry is the same work or a second related work. Accession numbers in the main group and sub-group may overlap. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Ink (pen) drawing on lined/ruled paper. Portrait-format sheet with a rectangular border drawn in ink in the upper portion of the sheet. Within the border: only the word "Деревня" (Village) written in large, flowing cursive script — no pictorial or visual content. The work exemplifies Malevich's Alogist approach — the word "Village" substitutes for a pictorial image of a village.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1916. Dimensions not given in the catalogue record — unusual for this sequence. Accession 147, URL prefix 85167. This is one of the most significant works in the dataset: a handwritten manifesto/declaration in Malevich's own hand, in red and black lettering on cream paper. The full text reads (in old pre-reform Russian orthography): "Я Апостол новыхъ понятій въ Искусствѣ / и Хирургъ Разума / стал на тронъ / Гордости творчества / и / Академію объявляю / Конюшней / Мѣщанъ" (I am the Apostle of New Concepts in Art / and Surgeon of the Mind / I have ascended the throne / of the Pride of Creativity / and / I declare the Academy / the Stable / of Philistines). Lower portion of sheet contains fragmentary black and red drawn/painted marks — possibly figures or abstract forms, partially cut off. This work functions simultaneously as a visual artwork and a polemical text. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Title: Alogisme 23. Sobol, koshka (Alogisme 23. Sabel, kat)
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1915. Accession 148, URL prefix 85168. Note: "Alogisme 23. Sobol, koshka" also appears in the Stedelijk's main 13xxx catalogue group — this 85xxx entry may be the same work photographed separately or a companion piece; requires verification. The composition is strongly vertical (15.1 × 5.6 cm) and divided into two labelled zones separated by a horizontal line — upper zone labelled "СОБОЛЬ" (Sable) containing a large downward-pointing dark triangle; lower zone labelled "КОШКА." (Cat) containing three dark squares in a row and a circle beside a cross-hatched square. This is pure Alogist logic: words substitute for or label geometric forms, denying conventional pictorial representation. A handwritten Russian annotation runs vertically down the right margin (partially legible): "алогъ / катил... / а белом не одирал... / а лагоне... / погул. нам бром. рдач. абогу" — a poetic or theoretical text. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Tall narrow portrait-format composition within a drawn rectangular border. The border is divided into two labelled registers by a horizontal line. records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1915. Accession number A 7683 — a completely different accession format from all other entries in this dataset (which use 4.2001(xxx) or similar); this is the Stedelijk's own collection accession number, not a Khardzhiev loan number. This work is NOT from the Khardzhiev collection — credits read "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008" (Ownership recognized by agreement with the estate of Kazimir Malevich in 2008), making this the only Stedelijk-owned Malevich work in the dataset. This is one of the most significant Malevich paintings in the Stedelijk's permanent collection. No misattribution issues noted from this record.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Portrait-format Suprematist painting on white ground. Six geometric forms arranged asymmetrically on a white ground: UPPER CENTRE — a large near-black square, roughly centred, dominant; LOWER LEFT GROUP — a tall yellow/ochre rectangle (vertical), a dark brown/maroon small square at its base, and a dark brown ring/annulus (circle with hole) to its right; LOWER RIGHT GROUP — a large cobalt blue tilted quadrilateral (diamond/rhombus form, rotated approximately 45°), and a small dark horizontal rectangle at its lower-right corner. The forms float freely on the white ground with no spatial depth or tonal graduation — pure flat colour. The palette is restrained: black, yellow-ochre, dark brown/maroon, cobalt blue, white. All edges are crisp and flat-painted. The painting exemplifies Malevich's mature Suprematist style of 1915. One of the most important works in the Stedelijk's permanent Malevich collection.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1907–1908. Accession 4.2001(002) — the second-lowest accession number in the Khardzhiev sequence, returning to the very beginning of the sub-series. URL prefix 12580 (not the main 13xxx group, different from the 85xxx sub-group). The work is a portrait sketch of the Russian composer Nikolai Roslavets (1881–1944), a figure associated with the Russian musical avant-garde. The subtitle "Песнь голубым облакам" (Song of the Blue Clouds) gives the work a Symbolist/Decadent quality — consistent with the Russian Symbolist movement of 1905–1910 in which Malevich was working before his Cubo-Futurist period. The composition — a nude figure playing violin before a stylised landscape — is strongly influenced by Art Nouveau/Symbolist aesthetics. Signed within the composition: "К. Малевич" in ink. TWO handwritten inscriptions below the border: "(Эскиз к портрету Рославца.) Песнь голуб. облакам." — the title in the artist's hand. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

The composition is strikingly sparse: against the warm amber ground, only a small number of elements float in the large empty field. UPPER AREA: a long diagonal bar (outline only, light grey) running from upper-left to lower-right; adjacent upper-right: two dark filled rectangles (one larger, one smaller) arranged in a stacked/parallel formation. CENTRE: a small dark cross or T-shaped element. LOWER-LEFT: a faint thin diagonal line (possibly a second overlapping bar, very lightly drawn). LOWER-CENTRE: a small grouped element — a horizontal rectangle with a tiny cross or bracket above it. LOWER-RIGHT within border: a small handwritten inscription, possibly "Мал" (abbreviated signature). A faint curved arc runs through the lower portion of the composition. The extreme emptiness and spatial openness of the composition — with forms scattered across a vast amber ground — evoke cosmic or architectural scale. The amber paper itself becomes an active ground rather than a neutral support.

This is the cover of the famous 1920 UNOVIS publication "Suprematizm. 34 risunka" (Suprematism. 34 Drawings) — one of the most important Suprematist publications, produced in Vitebsk by the UNOVIS group (Утвердители нового искусства / Affirmers of New Art) founded by Malevich. Malevich) in large block type; the title "СУПРЕМАТИЗМ" (Suprematism) in large bold type; subtitle "34 РИСУНКА" (34 drawings) in smaller type; a reproduced Black Square lower-left; the publisher imprint "УНОВИС / ВИТЕБСК 1920" (UNOVIS / Vitebsk 1920). This is a printed book/pamphlet rather than an original artwork — the image has a "NO REPRO QUALITY" watermark from the Stedelijk's image rights system, indicating the reproduction is restricted. 5 linked library documents. The UNOVIS group published this as a portfolio of 34 Suprematist lithographs. On the cover, a faint handwritten annotation is visible upper-centre (partially legible: "нем" or similar).

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas or board. Near-square format, no visible border or frame in the image. A richly coloured Symbolist/Neo-Primitivist figural composition. Three human figures — possibly female — are shown among or beneath large round fruit (pomegranates? oranges? exotic fruit) and dense foliage. The figures and fruit merge into a swirling, decorative whole: LEFT — a standing/upright blue-outlined figure facing the viewer, semi-nude, volumetric; CENTRE — a seated or crouching figure in yellow-green, with a more defined face; RIGHT — a third figure, partially obscured. The background is a dense, dark mass of rounded fruit forms and foliage in deep reds, oranges, purples, and blues. A basket or vessel appears lower-centre. The handling is thick and gestural — heavy impasto, bold colour contrasts. The overall atmosphere is lush, tropical, and Symbolist — influenced by Gauguin, Vrubel, and Russian Neo-Primitivism. One of the most colouristically rich works in the dataset alongside the Vrouw met krant (1904) and Nachtwandeling (1909–10).

Accession A 7659, classified as "Other". 23 linked library documents — the second highest in the dataset after A 7683 (40 documents). This is one of the most important Cubo-Futurist/Alogist paintings in the Stedelijk's Malevich collection, and one of the largest works in the dataset (92 × 92 cm square). The painting is signed lower-right "К. Малевич" — the seventh signed work in the dataset. Elements embedded in the composition include recognisable fragments: a calendar showing "29 / 6 / 7", a bottle label, a face (possibly a soldier or figure with a hat), grapes, circular/oval forms, and letters including "С А Л" (possibly "САЛО" = lard/suet, a Alogist verbal fragment). The composition is a Cubo-Futurist city scene — the tram stop of the title — decomposed into overlapping geometric planes.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Square format (92 × 92 cm) Cubo-Futurist/Alogist painting. A dense, complex composition of overlapping geometric planes, recognisable urban fragments, and text elements — a characteristic example of Malevich's Cubo-Futurist Alogist style of 1913–14. Colour palette: predominantly grey-blue and dark tones with punctuating areas of red-orange, green, yellow, purple, and white. Legible fragments embedded in the composition include: a CALENDAR page showing numbers "29 / 6 / 7" (centre); a white rectangle with a BOTTLE illustration (upper-centre); letters "С А Л" (upper-right) — possibly from "САЛО" (lard, a common Alogist verbal fragment); a FACE with moustache and hat (right); a green band with CIRCULAR forms; a FISH (right); GRAPES (lower-centre-right); an arc/wheel form (left). The fragmented, collage-like layering of urban everyday objects references both Analytical Cubism and the Russian Alogist tradition. Signed lower-right: "К. Малевич" in cursive. One of the most technically accomplished and iconographically complex paintings in the dataset.

records.Misattribution Notes: Two makers listed — Kazimir Malevich (designer) and El Lissitzky (designer). Accession 2000.1.0588 — a completely different format from all other accession numbers in the dataset, consistent with a library/archive acquisition. Date 1919. Classified as "Other". No credits listed. "O novykh sistemakh v iskusstve" (On New Systems in Art. Statics and Speed) is one of Malevich's major theoretical publications from the Vitebsk period — a manifesto-style text on Suprematism, statics, and speed, designed and lithographed in Vitebsk with El Lissitzky's involvement. The cover/page shown displays: (1) an epigraph in letterpress type at top: "«НИСПРОВЕРЖЕНИЕ СТАРОГО МИРА ИСКУССТВ ДА БУДЕТ ВЫЧЕРЧЕНО НА ВАШИХ ЛАДОНЯХ»" (Let the overthrow of the old world of art be scratched on your palms); (2) a framed Black Square print; (3) a diagonal text block left (title references "О НОВЫХ СИСТЕМАХ В ИСКУССТВЕ" / "СТАТИКА И СКОРОСТЬ"); (4) text "УСТАНОВЛЕНИЕ А" (Establishment A); (5) a framed circle print; (6) author name "МАЛЕВИЧК" (Malevichk — old orthography/abbreviation) below the circle. This is the second publication after the "Suprematizm. 34 risunka" (A 4481) to enter the dataset. 4 linked library documents.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "1920–1927". Stedelijk-owned work — credits: "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008". Accession A 7661, classified as "Other". 8 linked library documents. This is the fifth Stedelijk-owned oil painting in the dataset alongside A 7683, A 7648, A 7659, and A 7691. The work is exceptionally spare — a single cross form composed of just two thin bars (one black vertical, one dark red/brown horizontal) on a pure white ground. The white canvas ground has a faint blue atmospheric quality. The cross form directly connects this to the sustained cruciform iconographic thread in the dataset (4.2001(047), (048), (077), (119), (140)). The landscape-format canvas (67.5 × 83 cm) places the cross slightly right of centre and above the vertical midline — a subtle asymmetry that prevents it from reading as purely decorative. The extreme reductiveness — just two bars on white — places this among Malevich's most ascetic Suprematist works, related to the "white on white" period of 1918.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Landscape-format painting. An extremely spare Suprematist composition on a near-white ground. The canvas ground is white with a faint, atmospheric blue-grey mottling — suggesting infinite space rather than a neutral surface. Against this ground: a single cross form composed of exactly two bars — a tall, thin, flat black vertical bar; and a longer, thinner dark red/brown (brownish-red) horizontal bar crossing it asymmetrically, positioned slightly above the vertical bar's midpoint. The intersection of the two bars forms an asymmetric cross or plus-sign, placed slightly right of the canvas centre and in the upper half. The bars are flat-painted, edge-precise, with no shading or variation in tone. The extreme economy of means — two marks on white — places this among the most reductive Suprematist paintings in Malevich's oeuvre. The cross motif links it directly to the sustained cross iconography across the drawings in the dataset.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Portrait-format Suprematist painting on a white/off-white ground. The composition is bold, dynamic, and dramatically coloured. The ground has a faint atmospheric mottling (similar to A 7661). The main elements are: a large dark black circle positioned upper-centre, slightly left of the canvas centre axis; a bold, wide red vertical bar rising from below the canvas centre through and above the black circle, extending to the top edge; a bold, wide red horizontal bar crossing the vertical at approximately the level of the black circle's centre — forming a large asymmetric red cross overlaid on the black circle; LOWER LEFT — two small red rectangles stacked horizontally (one above the other, slightly offset); LOWER RIGHT — one wider red horizontal rectangle. The red elements below the cross are scattered asymmetrically, suggesting additional Suprematist elements in orbit or motion. The palette is restricted to three values: vivid cadmium red, absolute black, white. The scale and directness of the composition give it an iconic, almost heraldic quality — the cross over the circle reading as a cosmological symbol. This is the most visually commanding painting in the dataset.

Accession A 7655, classified as "Drawings" (anomalous — it is clearly an oil painting). No translated English title given in the catalogue record. 20 linked library documents. This is one of Malevich's most celebrated early figurative paintings — "De vloerboeners" (The Floor Polishers/Floor Scrubbers) — a Neo-Primitivist depiction of two male labourers. The work is signed lower-right: "К.Малев." (K. Malev[ich]) — abbreviated signature — the eighth signed work in the dataset. The large format (77.7 × 71 cm) and bold, flat colour palette (yellow, red, green, blue-grey, pink, ochre) are characteristic of the Russian Neo-Primitivist movement of 1910–1913. The painting directly relates to the "Bader" (1911) and "Baadsters op de rug gezien" (1910) works listed in "More work from this maker" — all early figurative Neo-Primitivist paintings from the same period. This work is likely the most historically significant early painting in the dataset after the 1904 Impressionist portrait.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on cream/buff paper. Tall narrow portrait-format composition within a drawn rectangular border — the most elongated format in the dataset (approximately 2.5:1 height-to-width ratio). A dense Cubist composition depicting a wall clock decomposed into overlapping faceted planes. The clock subject is legible through fragments: UPPER — a large circular clock face with Roman numerals (XII clearly visible), clock hands, and a decorative surround; a pendulum or weight element; MIDDLE/LOWER — the clock case/housing rendered in multiple overlapping geometric planes, prismatic and faceted. The composition fills the entire bordered field with no empty space — densely worked throughout. Tonal range from white through mid-grey to near-black. The diagonal faceting and multiple simultaneous viewpoints are characteristic of Analytical Cubism adapted to a Russian context. Signed lower-right below the border: "К.Мал." (abbreviated signature). A complex, multi-layered Alogist/Cubo-Futurist stage design combining pencil drawing and applied black rectangular blocks. Accession A 33381(1-18) — a group accession of 18 sheets, completely unique in the dataset. No dimensions given. URL prefix 102321 — a new prefix, the highest number yet seen. Classified as "Drawings". 14 linked library documents. This is Malevich's theoretical "Supplementary Element" chart series — part of his systematic Bauhaus-influenced art theory developed at GINKhUK (State Institute of Artistic Culture, Leningrad) and later related to his 1927 Bauhaus book. The chart shown divides into three sections: I "Виды произведений" (Types of Works) numbered 1-8; II "Анализ ощущений" (Analysis of Sensations) numbered 9-16; III "Прагматический метод" (Pragmatic Method) numbered 17-22. Each numbered cell contains small diagrams. Below each section: explanatory text paragraphs. At the bottom: institutional signatures — "В исследовании работают: / Проф. К.С. Малевич / Аспиранты: Д.М. Рощенко, Л.М. Юдин, А.А. Лепорская, Л.М. Хидекель..." (In the research work: / Prof. K.S. Malevich / Graduate students...). This is a collaborative institutional document, not a solo artwork. Title of the chart reads at top: "План развески графиков исследований произведений культуры / Исследование живописи к культуре каким образом культурно здоровый..." On loan/owned by Stedelijk.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Nearly square format (77 × 79 cm). A close-up, frontal figural composition — a single female figure seen from the bust up, surrounded by abundant fruit. The figure dominates the canvas: a large pale blue-green face with simplified but readable features (eyes, nose, mouth, cheek marks); flowing dark blue hair; a voluminous rounded body rendered in swirling blue-white impasto strokes. The hands/arms are spread wide, cradling two fruits — a dark blue-purple sphere (left) and a bright yellow-orange sphere (right). The surrounding space is densely filled with fruit and foliage: grapes (dark blue-purple, upper-left), pears (red-brown, upper-right), various round and oblong fruits, leaves (amber, brown, orange, dark green, blue-red). The background is completely filled — no empty space visible. The painterly handling is thick and energetic — swirling brushstrokes in the figure area contrast with the more articulated fruit and leaf forms in the surround. The palette is dominated by blue-green (figure) against warm amber-brown and orange (fruit/background). The most intimate and psychologically direct of the three 1909 fruit/figure works in the dataset.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "ca. 1923". Accession 5.2001(848) [voormalige coll.] — third entry with the "5.2001" former-collection prefix (alongside 5.2001(849) MAL-222 and 5.2001(886) MAL-223). Note: accession 848 is consecutive with 849 (MAL-222 Grafik dvizheniya), suggesting these two were catalogued together. Credits: "overgedragen aan RGALI (Russian State Archive of Literature and Art), Moskou" — transferred to RGALI Moscow. Classified as "Other". 2 linked library documents. The title "Творчество не может быть свободно" (Creativity Cannot Be Free) is a significant theoretical statement — a deliberate inversion of the Romantic/liberal notion of creative freedom. This appears to be a handwritten document or drawing related to Malevich's GINKhUK theoretical writings of the early 1920s, consistent in date and provenance with MAL-222. URL prefix 92252.

records.Title: Twee mannen in beweging
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "1917–1918 of ca. 1930" — the most ambiguous dating in the dataset, spanning 12+ years with a decisive stylistic/chronological gap. Accession 4.2001(058) — FILLS THE LAST OUTSTANDING GAP in the flagged sequence. Previously listed outstanding gaps: 058, 051, 071, 072, 078. With 051 and 058 now filled, remaining outstanding: 071, 072, 078. URL prefix 2132 — one of the lowest URL prefix numbers in the dataset, suggesting an early catalogue entry. 2 linked library documents. The composition — two simplified figurative forms in movement — is consistent with both the 1918 figurative series (featureless oval-headed figures) and the ca. 1930 late figurative works. The dating ambiguity reflects this visual overlap. The composition is placed in the upper-right quadrant of a large graph paper sheet, with most of the sheet left empty — similar to the Compositie 2 t (MAL-210). On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on graph/squared paper. Landscape-format sheet — the drawing occupies only the upper-right quadrant of the larger sheet, with the remaining three-quarters entirely blank. The composition is within a drawn rectangular border. Two simplified figurative forms in a dynamic, moving pose: LEFT/FRONT figure — a darker, more shaded form with an oval head (no facial features), leaning forward in motion, legs spread, one arm holding what appears to be a small oval object (racquet? tool?); RIGHT/BACK figure — a lighter, less defined outline form of a similar figure, slightly behind and to the right. Both figures are in a striding, athletic pose suggesting movement or sport. The forms are rendered in soft pencil with gentle tonal shading — the darker front figure is modelled, the lighter rear figure is more schematic. The featureless oval heads and simplified tubular limbs connect this to both the 1917–1918 theatrical figure series and the 1930 late figurative works. Graph paper grid visible throughout.

records.Title: Troye (Трое)
records.Misattribution Notes: Multiple makers: Malevich (designer/ontwerper), Khlebnikov (author), Kruchenykh (author), Guro (author), Matyushin (publisher). Accession 1998.1.0183 — library/archive format, consistent with a 1998 acquisition. No credits listed. Classified as "Other". 14 linked library documents — among the highest in the dataset. Date 1913. "Troye" (The Three) is a major Futurist miscellany publication — poems by Khlebnikov, Kruchenykh, and Elena Guro, published by Matyushin in 1913. This is the most extensively collaborated work in the dataset (five named makers). The cover shows Malevich's design: bold black letterpress/lithograph title "ТРОЕ" (Troye) in large fragmented letters; a central Neo-Primitivist figure (a compact, cubified peasant or worker figure seen from behind, rendered in flat black); lower-left: handwritten author credits "В. Хлебников / А. Хруч[еных]"; lower-right: "Е. Гуро" (E. Guro); a small monogram "К.М." (Kazimir Malevich) visible centre-right. The cover design integrates Malevich's Neo-Primitivist figurative style with bold typographic Futurism.

records.Image: Notes: Photograph of the cover of the Futurist publication "Troye" (Трое / The Three), 1913. The cover is printed in black on cream/off-white card stock, slightly worn at edges. DESIGN: bold black lithographed/letterpress title "ТРОЕ" (Troye) in very large, fragmented, quasi-typographic letters filling the upper half of the cover — the letters are bold, angular, and energetically composed. CENTRE — a compact, blocky Neo-Primitivist figure seen from a three-quarter rear view: a squat, solid form with a hat/cap, coat, and feet firmly planted — rendered in flat black with minimal detail. A small horizontal bar beneath the figure. Lower-right of the figure: the monogram "К.М." (Kazimir Malevich). LOWER-LEFT — handwritten author credits in cursive: "В. Хлебников / А. Хрученых" (V. Khlebnikov / A. Kruchenykh). LOWER-RIGHT — "Е. Гуро" (E. Guro). The cover is a major example of early Russian Futurist book design, combining Malevich's Neo-Primitivist figuration with bold typographic invention.

records.Title: Composition 1 e (Suprematisme: vierkant op diagonaal vlak)
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1915. Accession 4.2001(020), URL prefix 11731. 3 linked library documents. Khardzhiev loan. The composition is one of the clearest illustrations of early Suprematist compositional logic: a large diagonal trapezoid/wedge form (shaded in pencil hatching) fills the left portion of the bordered field, with a small black square placed at its lower-right corner — the black square being Suprematism's foundational element. The right portion of the field is left completely empty. The title describes this precisely: "Composition 1 e (Suprematism: Square on a Diagonal Surface)" — the "e" may refer to a compositional type within a numbered series. The composition demonstrates how the Black Square motif can be deployed within a larger geometric field, rather than in isolation. On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on amber/buff card stock. Portrait-format composition within a drawn rectangular border on a larger amber sheet. The composition is asymmetric and spare: LEFT — a large diagonal trapezoid or wedge form, its left edge vertical and its right edge diagonal (running from upper-centre to lower-left), filled with dense horizontal pencil hatching — dark grey throughout; at the lower-right corner of this hatched form sits a small solid black square (darker than the hatching, filled). RIGHT — the remainder of the bordered field is entirely empty/white. A faint curved line is visible in the right portion (possibly an erased mark or paper feature). The composition demonstrates the early Suprematist approach of 1915: the diagonal plane as a ground for the Black Square motif. Amber card, no grid.

records.Title: Suprematistische compositie (met gele, oranje en groene rechthoek)
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date "1915–1916". Stedelijk-owned work — credits: "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008". Accession A 7675, classified as "Other". 21 linked library documents — the third highest in the dataset after A 7683 (40) and A 7669 (34). The eighth Stedelijk-owned oil painting in the dataset. A classic mature Suprematist composition: the palette is vivid — yellow/ochre, orange-red, teal/green, black, blue — with forms floating freely on a near-white ground. The Stedelijk title notes "yellow, orange and green rectangle" but the composition also includes two tall black vertical bars, a horizontal black bar, and two small blue horizontal elements. The combination of overlapping large rectangles (yellow, red/orange, teal/green) with slender black bars is typical of the 1915–1916 Suprematist peak.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas. Portrait-format Suprematist painting on a near-white/off-white ground. A classic multi-element Suprematist composition with forms floating freely: LARGE FORMS — a yellow/ochre tilted square or rectangle (upper-left, rotated approximately 15°); overlapping it, an orange-red L-shaped or angular rectangle (centre-left, partially behind the yellow); a large teal/dark green rectangle (centre-right, approximately square, slightly tilted); a second smaller teal rectangle (right, partially behind the first). SLENDER FORMS — two tall black vertical bars (centre-upper, closely spaced, one slightly taller); a longer diagonal/horizontal black bar (lower, running left to right across the lower third). SMALL FORMS — two short blue horizontal elements (lower-left, one dark, one medium blue, stacked). The palette is vivid: yellow-ochre, orange-red, teal-green, black, blue, on white. The composition is asymmetric and dynamic — the overlapping large rectangles create depth, while the black bars add tension and verticality. One of the most colouristically rich Suprematist oil paintings in the dataset.

records.Title: Engelsman in Moskou
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1913–1914. Accession 4.2001(1615) — by far the highest accession number in the Khardzhiev sequence in the dataset (previous highest: 4.2001(172)). URL prefix 99430 — very high. No translated English title in the catalogue record (Dutch title only: "Engelsman in Moskou" = Englishman in Moscow). 3 linked library documents. The image shows a two-page sketchbook spread: LEFT PAGE — a complex Alogist/Cubo-Futurist drawing with embedded text fragments: "ЗА / ТМЕ" (upper right of composition), "НЕ" (centre), "ЧА / СТИЧНОЕ" (lower — together "ЗАТМЕНИЕ / ЧАСТИЧНОЕ" = Partial Eclipse — this is likely a study for or related to the Alogisme 3 "Chastichnoe zatmenie" (Partial Eclipse) series already in the dataset); an arrow pointing left (upper); a fish, an eye/face fragment, a spoon, a candle, and other Alogist objects. RIGHT PAGE — a full page of handwritten Russian theoretical text in blue ink, partially legible: "мои картины к моде / то не в каталоге / является заставкой / три разума зрителя / снимкута с старого / фундамента, принятого / жение то его старый / горшок разум." (My paintings and fashion / not in a catalogue / is a header / three minds of the viewer / removed from the old / foundation, accepted / his old / pot of reason.) On loan from Stichting Khardzhiev.

records.Image: Resolution: Screenshot at screen resolution — two-page sketchbook spread shown
records.Image: Notes: Two-sided image: RECTO (left) — pencil on paper, 14 × 10 cm. A preliminary sketch for "An Englishman in Moscow" in Cubo-Futurist/Alogist style. Dense composition of overlapping fragmented forms: a fish, a spoon, an eye, a candle, a top hat, ladder/stave forms, architectural elements, and bold Cyrillic text fragments: "ЗА ТМЕ" (upper right), "НИЕ" (centre), "ЧА" (lower left), "СТИЧНОЕ" (lower). These Russian text fragments spell "ЗАТМЕНИЕ" (zatmenie = eclipse) and "ЧАСТИЧНОЕ" (chastichnoe = partial) — read together: "ЧАСТИЧНОЕ ЗАТМЕНИЕ" (Partial Eclipse), directly referencing Malevich's Alogist painting of the same title. A pencil border frames the composition. VERSO (right) — handwritten Russian text in Malevich's hand, multiple lines, covering the full right half of the sheet. Text begins: "Мои картины и то же / что их в каталогт / являются заставленной / зря разум зрителя / свинегутся с сторого / фундамента, принятя / жние то ею старьи / горшоки разумь." (Partial transcription — theoretical/philosophical statement about Malevich's paintings and the viewer's rational mind.) Additional faint pencil sketches visible on verso lower half (partially legible geometric/figure studies). Khardzhiev loan item 1615 — highest confirmed item number in collection.

records.Title: Toekomstige planits voor Leningrad. Het huis van de vliegenier
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1924. Stedelijk-owned work — credits: "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008". Accession A 7698, classified as "Drawings". 13 linked library documents. The ninth Stedelijk-owned work in the dataset (alongside A 7683, A 7648, A 7659, A 7661, A 7669, A 7675, A 7691, A 7697). A 7698 is the last in the A 769x series. This is Malevich's famous "Planit" (Планит) series — architectural designs for three-dimensional Suprematist structures intended as future housing. "Planit" is a portmanteau of "плоскость" (plane) and "планета" (planet). The specific design shown — "Het huis van de vliegenier" (The Pilot's House) — is one of the most architecturally specific Planit designs. Multiple handwritten annotations: top of sheet: "Супрефорна [?] а 3 группа баналов" (partially legible); right margin: "Планит [?] [?] будущего / Ленинграда" (Planit of the Future / of Leningrad); lower-centre: "к.м. 1924г." (abbreviation + year); bottom below border: "Планит лётчика [?]" (Planit of the Aviator/Pilot). The isometric axonometric projection is drawn with precision — three-dimensional stacked and projecting rectangular elements forming a stepped/tiered architectural mass.

records.Image: Notes: Pencil drawing on amber/buff paper. Landscape-format composition within a drawn rectangular border (with an additional diagonal line in the upper-right corner of the border creating a triangular sub-zone). A highly precise architectural axonometric projection of a Planit (Suprematist three-dimensional structure). The structure is drawn in isometric view, showing a complex stepped and cantilevered assembly of rectangular volumes: VERTICAL ELEMENT — a tall central spine of stacked dark (hatched) and light (outline) rectangular slabs diminishing upward; HORIZONTAL ELEMENTS — a series of wide horizontal bars projecting left and right at different levels, with alternating dark and light (hatched/outline) treatment; the overall form suggests a stepped pyramid or ziggurat-like structure viewed from slightly above and to the right. The three-dimensional quality is achieved through careful axonometric projection without perspective. Above the border: handwritten Russian annotation (partially legible). Right margin outside border: "Планит [?] будущего / Ленинграда" (Planit of the Future Leningrad). Lower-right within border: "к.м. 1924г." Below border: "Планит лётчика [?]" (Planit of the Aviator/Pilot). Amber/buff paper.

records.Title: Suprematisme van de geest
records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1919. Accession 4.2001(001) — lowest number in the Khardzhiev sequence. URL prefix 12124. 15 linked library documents — among the highest in the dataset. Classified as "Other". Double loan credit: "bruikleen Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed en Stichting Khardzhiev / on loan from the Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands and Stichting Khardzhiev" — the only work in the dataset with dual loan credit (both the Dutch state cultural heritage agency and the Khardzhiev Foundation). This is the "Suprematism of the Spirit" panel, painted in Vitebsk in 1919. Lissitzky called it "the crucified square". The cross-arms consist of intersecting rectangular planes. Khardzhiev acquired this work and it became, according to the Khardzhiev catalogue, a reason for him to move his collection to Amsterdam and establish a Malevich study centre there. 84 × 66 cm, 7 cm depth — indicating a substantial panel, not paper. A unique object in the dataset: the only 3D panel work (as opposed to flat drawing/painting on canvas/paper). URL prefix 12124 (confirmed). Joint loan from Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed AND Stichting Khardzhiev — dual-agency loan, distinct from single-agency Khardzhiev loans (4.2001 series). Image now available — screenshot captured 12 April 2026.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on panel, 84 × 66 × 7 cm. Portrait format. The 7 cm depth confirms this is a thick wooden panel, not canvas. A Suprematist composition on a pale grey-white ground. COMPOSITION: Two distinct sub-groups of geometric elements separated by empty space: UPPER GROUP — a large white/off-white square or rectangular plane (centre), slightly tilted, overlapping with: a tall vertical black rectangle above (upper-centre, extending above the white plane); a short cream/buff vertical strip below the black bar (connecting the bar to the white square); a short horizontal black bar (left, mid-height, extending leftward from the white plane edge); a longer horizontal black bar (right, mid-height, extending rightward beyond the white plane). LOWER GROUP — below the midpoint of the canvas: a vertical black bar (centre, extending downward); a cream/buff vertical strip overlapping the black bar (same axis, slightly offset); a diagonal orange/amber bar crossing the black bar from lower-left to right. GROUND: pale cool grey-white, with visible painted surface texture. PALETTE: black, white/off-white, cream/buff, orange/amber — restrained four-colour palette. The composition has strong cruciform/cross associations — two vertical black bars with crossing horizontals, connecting to Malevich's cross-as-Suprematist-symbol theme of 1919–1920. 15 library documents. Joint loan: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed AND Stichting Khardzhiev — unusual dual-agency loan, not purely Khardzhiev. URL prefix 12124.

records.Image: Notes:
Gouache or tempera on paper (medium not confirmed in catalogue), 27.8 × 27.8 cm. Near-square format. A fully painted, richly coloured figurative composition — NOT a pencil drawing as previously recorded. 
COMPOSITION: A large nude figure seen from behind, seated or crouching, filling most of the square format. The figure is shown from a close, slightly elevated viewpoint — back, buttocks, and bent legs dominate. HEAD — small, dark green/teal, near-circular, shown in left profile at top-centre; no facial features visible. BODY — the back, shoulders, and torso are rendered in bold yellow/lemon and deep red/crimson alternating planes, separated by thick dark (navy/black) outlines in the manner of Matisse/Gauguin. The skin tones are non-naturalistic: bright yellow-lemon for the lit surfaces, deep red-crimson for the shadow and modelled areas, with white highlights on the spine and shoulder blade areas. LEGS — bent beneath the figure; lower legs and feet visible at bottom; yellow and red tones continuing. A white cloth or surface lies beneath/around the lower figure — bottom-centre and lower-left. BACKGROUND — the entire background is a warm, vibrant red-orange, painted with circular/spiral brushwork (reminiscent of Van Gogh or Cézannist texture) — swirling warm reds and oranges filling the upper and left areas. LOWER RIGHT — a green and dark blue-navy area with leaf/plant forms (green foliage and blue-purple stone/earth forms) — a landscape element contrasting with the warm red background. UPPER RIGHT — a dark near-black area (tree trunk or dark mass). PALETTE — yellow/lemon, deep red/crimson, dark green, dark navy/blue-purple, white, orange-red, black outlines. Bold, non-naturalistic colour throughout — strongly Fauvist/Gauguin-influenced. 
MEDIUM NOTE: The work is clearly painted (not pencil) — broad colour areas, painted outlines, no pencil line visible. The Stedelijk catalogue lists as "Drawings" and medium is absent — both are cataloguing errors or anomalies. This work is closely related to the Bader (A 7653, MAL-238) in subject, date, and style — both are 1910–11 bather compositions in the Cézanne/Matisse/Gauguin tradition. Unlike Bader (which shows the figure from the front/three-quarter), this shows the figure strictly from behind — a classic Cézannist back-view bather motif. Khardzhiev loan item 087.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas, 60.2 × 51.6 cm. Near-square format canvas. A pure Suprematist composition — eight red rectangles of varying sizes and proportions arranged in a dynamic diagonal sweep across a white/off-white textured ground. COMPOSITION: The rectangles are distributed across the canvas in a loose diagonal running from lower-left to upper-right. Elements include: two large squares/near-squares (upper-left cluster); two long horizontal bars (centre, sweeping diagonally); one tall vertical/diagonal rectangle (upper-right, the largest single element — extending off-canvas at right edge); two small rectangles (centre-left cluster); one medium rectangle (lower-centre-right). All eight elements share the same deep red/crimson colour — a single hue, no tonal variation or modelling. GROUND: off-white/cream with visible canvas texture and aged surface — not a flat white but a worked, slightly warm ground. The composition conveys strong sensation of movement and floating — no element is orthogonal to the canvas edge; all are slightly rotated, contributing to the dynamic energy. Monochromatic palette (red on white only). First exhibited at 0.10 exhibition Petrograd December 1915. 58 related library documents — highest confirmed document count in the dataset.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas, 105 × 65.7 cm. Portrait-format canvas. A dynamic multi-element Suprematist composition in two distinct registers: UPPER HALF — dominated by a very large black diamond/square rotated approximately 45° (set on its corner), occupying the upper-centre and right of the composition. On top of and overlapping the black diamond: a large yellow/ochre rectangle (horizontal, centre of diamond); a blue rectangle (centre-right); a dark red/maroon diagonal bar crossing the yellow; two small red elements (upper-right, outside diamond: a small square and two short bars); a green horizontal bar (lower edge of yellow). UPPER-LEFT — outside the black diamond: three short dark diagonal strokes/bars and one small dark square, floating freely on the white ground. MIDDLE — separating the two registers: two long thin diagonal lines crossing the canvas (one black, one dark red/maroon), running roughly parallel from left to right. LOWER HALF — on the white ground: a large red square (centre, the dominant lower element); multiple yellow/ochre horizontal bars of varying lengths radiating from the red square; a dark brown/maroon short bar (right of red square); one short black bar (lower-right); one small blue rectangle (lower-right); one small green rectangle (lower-right, bottom). Palette: black, yellow/ochre, blue, red, green, dark red/maroon, white. A richly coloured and compositionally complex Suprematist painting — one of the most elaborate multi-element works in the Stedelijk Malevich collection.

records.Image: Notes: Oil on canvas, 91.7 × 72 × 4.3 cm. Portrait format. A white-on-grey Suprematist composition — the White Suprematist Cross. COMPOSITION: A large Greek cross (equal-arm cross) occupies nearly the full canvas surface. The cross arms are broad and centred: one vertical arm running full height, one horizontal arm running full width, intersecting at the centre. CROSS — rendered in a bright, slightly warm white with visible painterly brushwork; surface texture is uneven with directional strokes. GROUND — the four corner quadrants flanking the cross arms are a cool blue-grey/silver-grey, subtly distinct from the cross. Both cross and ground have a heavily worked, textured surface with visible craquelure and paint application marks — fully consistent with a 1920–21 oil painting now over 100 years old. The distinction between cross and ground is tonal only — both within the white/grey register, no colour contrast. NO sharp edges — boundaries between cross and ground are soft, painted rather than masked. The overall surface has a mottled, atmospheric quality — painterly rather than geometric-precise. PALETTE: white (cross), cool blue-grey (ground). 30 library documents. Accession A 7667 confirmed. Part of Sandberg 1958 acquisition.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1920–1921. Stedelijk-owned work — "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008 / Ownership recognized by agreement with the estate of Kazimir Malevich in 2008". Accession A 7667, URL prefix 2173. 30 linked library documents — among the highest document counts in the dataset, reflecting the importance of this work. Classified as "Other". 91.7 × 72 × 4.3 cm — a substantial canvas. "White Suprematist Cross" — painted 1920–1921, this work belongs to Malevich's late Suprematist / white-on-white period, following the breakthrough White on White (1918). The composition shows a large white cross form set against a slightly different white/pale grey ground — the cross rendered in a warmer or brighter white than the four corner quadrants, which are a cooler grey-white or pale blue-grey. The cross arms are broad, centred, and orthogonal (upright, not diagonal). The entire surface is worked with painterly brushwork rather than flat geometric precision — consistent with Malevich's post-1918 approach in which surface texture and chromatic nuance within the white field became expressive elements. This is the only "white cross" work in the Stedelijk Malevich dataset. The date 1920–1921 locates it in the Vitebsk/early Petrograd period, when Malevich was developing the cross motif as a culminating Suprematist symbol. Note: A 7667 falls between A 7666 (White Planes in Dissolution) and A 7668 (not yet recorded) in the accession sequence — confirming its place in the 1958 Sandberg acquisition group.

records.Image: Notes:
Drawing, 36 × 53.5 cm. Landscape-format work on warm ochre/tan paper or card. SUPPORT: the ground is a warm buff/ochre — either naturally coloured paper or card, or aged paper. A pencil (and possibly light ink) architectural drawing executed in isometric/axonometric projection. 
COMPOSITION: A complex Suprematist architectural structure — an Arkhitekton-type composition — depicted as a three-dimensional isometric drawing, viewed from slightly above and to the right (bird's-eye oblique). The structure consists of multiple interlocking horizontal rectangular volumes (slabs, bars, and blocks) of varying heights and lengths, arranged along a dominant diagonal axis running from lower-left to upper-right. 
STRUCTURE ELEMENTS: A central tall/wide block (the primary vertical mass, upper-centre); multiple long low horizontal slabs extending left and right; several shorter accent blocks; a freestanding rectangular block to the lower-left (isolated, lower). The forms are rendered in pencil outline with areas of dark shading (graphite or dark pencil, near-black) applied to specific faces — rooftops and side faces — to create the illusion of depth and shadow. The unshaded faces are left as the bare ochre paper colour, creating a two-tone effect: dark (shaded) vs warm buff (light faces). 
ANNOTATIONS: Handwritten Russian text at top centre of the sheet — the title "Сегодняшние сооружения" (Segodnyashnye sooruzheniya / Today's/Modern Buildings/Structures) in Malevich's hand. Below the drawing, two lines of handwritten Russian text (a note or caption, partially legible): begins "Супрем." (Suprematism/Suprematist) followed by further text — likely a theoretical statement or description. A faint pencil border/frame rectangle encloses the drawing area. 
MEDIUM NOTE: The drawing is executed with precision consistent with architectural draughtsmanship — straight lines, consistent line weight, careful shading. The warm ochre support gives the whole sheet a unified warm tone. The shading technique — parallel pencil strokes on horizontal roof faces — is consistent across all volumes. This is one of the most architecturally explicit works in the dataset, directly evidencing Malevich's Suprematist architectural theory in drawn form.

records.Image: Notes:
Medium not specified; likely gouache or tempera on paper, 26.3 × 26.4 cm. Near-square format. A densely painted, luminous Symbolist/proto-Expressionist composition dominated entirely by a warm golden-yellow/amber tonality. 
COMPOSITION: Centrally organised in a hierarchical, icon-like arrangement. CENTRAL FIGURE — a seated or enthroned saint/holy figure occupies the centre of the composition: shown frontally, cross-legged (lotus-like posture), arms raised and spread outward in an orant or welcoming gesture. The figure has reddish-orange hair; two small red/orange circular marks at the temples or forehead (possibly a halo detail or stigmata-like marks); a serene, simplified face. The figure merges into the golden ground — body rendered in warm amber/ochre tones barely distinguishable from the background, creating a dissolution-into-light effect. SURROUNDING FIELD — the entire ground is a rich, textured golden-yellow, painted with dense circular/mosaic-like brushwork suggesting a shimmering, Byzantine-gold ground. ATTENDANT FIGURES — multiple smaller figures distributed around the central saint in a hierarchical arrangement: LEFT and RIGHT sides — clusters of smaller figures (worshippers or angels), rendered in warm amber/ochre with green-tinged areas, showing faces in profile or three-quarter view; LOWER semicircle — a row of smaller figures with circular halos/heads, evenly spaced, facing inward toward the central figure; UPPER register — additional small figures distributed across the top, with two teal/blue-green curving forms (possibly clouds or angelic wings) flanking the upper centre. A single small blue/teal arc is visible at the very top centre. GREEN ACCENTS — two broad green curving strokes frame the central figure's raised arms, suggesting a mandorla or aura of a different colour. PALETTE — almost exclusively warm golden-yellow/amber, with accents of: orange-red (hair, marks), green-teal (mandorla, upper elements), and minimal blue. The surface has a mosaic-like or pointillist texture across the golden ground, suggesting Divisionist influence. ICONOGRAPHIC CONTEXT — the composition closely follows the structure of Orthodox icon painting: central enthroned/ascending holy figure, hierarchical arrangement of attendants, gold ground, orant gesture, mandorla. The "Assumption" subject (bodily ascent to heaven) is a canonical subject in both Russian Orthodox and Ukrainian Greek Catholic iconography — directly connected to Malevich's Ukrainian upbringing. This is one of the earliest works in the dataset (1907–08) and one of the most iconographically complex.

records.Image: Notes:
Gouache or tempera on paper (medium not confirmed in catalogue), 11 × 11 cm. Miniature square format — smallest work in the dataset. A fully painted, luminous Symbolist composition in a warm yellow-green and orange palette. 
COMPOSITION: Centrally organised. A single standing nude figure dominates the centre of the square. FIGURE — shown full-length, frontally, arms raised straight above the head, hands open and upward. The figure is rendered in a flat teal/sage green — fully desaturated, non-naturalistic skin tone, merging partially with the yellow-green ground. The body is slender, simplified, without detailed modelling. HEAD — small, with reddish-orange hair visible; a pale circular disc or halo directly above the head (also readable as the sun being held aloft). At the pubic area: a small orange/terracotta triangle. SOLAR DISC — above and between the raised hands: a large pale white/cream circular form with a slightly textured/luminous surface — the sun or a radiant orb. It is set into a warmer orange-gold area at the top-centre, suggesting a glowing sky or aureole. BACKGROUND — the entire ground is a warm olive/yellow-green. LEFT and RIGHT flanking the figure: large rounded orange forms (foliage, clouds, or flames) — warm orange-red organic masses with teal/green leaf-like accents. The orange masses are framed by teal/sage green leaf and tendril forms extending from the edges. A curved pale yellow/cream path or ground plane wraps around the lower portion of the figure — an elliptical light zone framing the figure's feet and lower body. Scattered across the ground: small rounded teal-green forms (pebbles, flowers, or leaves). Small flower-like elements in yellow-green visible lower-left and lower-right. Small black ink floral/plant details at lower-left. 
STYLE: Dense, jewel-like surface quality; the yellow-green ground and orange flanking masses recall both Russian Symbolism and Jugendstil/Art Nouveau decorative painting. The palette (yellow-green, teal, orange) is identical in character to Tenhemelopneming van een heilige (MAL-242, 1907–08, same Khardzhiev batch) — confirming a coherent early Symbolist series. The subject — a human figure raising arms to the sun — directly anticipates "Victory over the Sun" (1913). Despite the miniature scale (11 × 11 cm), the image is richly detailed and fully resolved.

records.Image: Notes:
Pencil and ink on paper (medium inferred), 39 × 29.5 cm. Portrait-format sheet on cream/off-white paper with aged surface. The most complex and document-like architectural drawing in the dataset — a multi-view compositional sheet containing several distinct elements: 
MAIN DRAWING (upper centre): A large axonometric/plan-view drawing of a Planit composition, enclosed within a dashed or lightly ruled rectangular border. The plan shows a Suprematist architectural complex viewed from directly above — multiple dark rectangular forms (black/dark graphite) arranged in a dynamic diagonal pattern on a white ground: a large central dark rectangle (horizontal), flanked by shorter perpendicular bars, with a long diagonal bar extending lower-right, and smaller accent forms. The composition is strongly reminiscent of a Suprematist painting translated into an architectural floor plan. A long vertical pencil line extends from the top of the plan downward through the sheet — possibly a plumb line or axial reference. 
LEFT MARGIN: A small separate sketch — a side elevation or section view of the structure, showing stacked horizontal volumes. 
RIGHT MARGIN: Another small sketch — a three-quarter perspective view or elevation of the structure showing the massing. 
LOWER SECTION: Three distinct elements: (1) A text block in Russian (several lines of handwritten text — theoretical/descriptive caption); (2) A small inset box lower-left containing a simplified plan or elevation sketch; (3) A larger text block lower-right with multiple lines of Russian handwriting — the most extensive text annotation in the architectural subset. 
HEADER ANNOTATIONS: At the top of the sheet, above the main drawing: handwritten Russian title text in two lines — "Планit" (Planit) visible, followed by the full title description. A date annotation "1920–1924" or similar appears below the title. 
The sheet annotation "л.4" (leaf/page 4) appears lower-right of the main drawing — confirming this is sheet 4 of a multi-sheet series. This connects it to MAL-240 (Segodnyashnye sooruzheniya) which has similar annotation structure — together they form part of a numbered series of architectural drawings. The extensive Russian text annotations are entirely uncatalogued in the Stedelijk record.

records.Misattribution Notes: Nationality label absent from Stedelijk record. Date 1912. Stedelijk-owned work — "Eigendom erkend door erven Malevich bij overeenkomst uit 2008 / Ownership recognized by agreement with the estate of Kazimir Malevich in 2008". URL prefix 3138. Accession A 7678 (confirmed). 19 linked library documents. Translated title: "Taking in the Rye" (Dutch: Oogstende vrouwen/Het binnenhalen van de rogge II — literally "Harvesting women/Taking in the rye II"). The "II" suffix indicates this is the second version of this composition — a first version exists elsewhere. Stedelijk classifies as "Other" — anomalous for an oil on canvas painting (compare De vloerboeners/MAL-236-area, also classified as "Drawings"). Near-square format (72 × 74.5 cm). Date 1912 — this is a key transitional year for Malevich, between his Neo-Primitivist peasant series (1910–12) and his Cubo-Futurist alogist period (1913–14). The harvesting/rye subject is drawn directly from Ukrainian peasant agricultural life — a subject with deep personal resonance for Malevich, who grew up in sugar-beet farming communities in Ukraine. The cylindrical/tubular figure treatment (arms like rolled cylinders, bodies as geometric tubes) is characteristic of Malevich's 1912 "peasant cycle" — a style strongly influenced by Léger's tubism and Gleizes/Metzinger's Cubism, but applied to Ukrainian rural subject matter. This work is closely related to: "Kososnitsa" (The Reaper), "Oogst" (Harvest), and "Vrouwen op het veld" (Women in the Field) — all 1912 Stedelijk works in the same series. The peasant-harvest subject directly connects to Malevich's Ukrainian heritage — agricultural labour, specifically rye harvesting, was the economic basis of the Ukrainian communities where he grew up. This connection is entirely absent from the Stedelijk record. Nationality entirely absent — ninety-sixth consecutive Stedelijk omission.

records.Image: Notes:
Oil on canvas, 72 × 74.5 cm. Near-square format. Framed (narrow dark frame visible at edges). A richly coloured Neo-Primitivist/Cubo-Futurist peasant composition depicting three female figures engaged in harvesting rye. 
FIGURES: Three women in dynamic bending/stooping postures, filling the canvas from edge to edge. LEFT FIGURE — largest, facing right and bending forward; wearing a white blouse/top and red skirt; red rounded head (no facial features visible, head as geometric form); arms extended reaching forward. CENTRE-UPPER FIGURE — shown from behind, bending deeply forward; wearing a blue dress/top with white highlights; dark rounded head; arms reaching down. RIGHT-LOWER FIGURE — bent most dramatically, head nearly touching the lower centre; wearing a mauve/purple top and dark teal/green skirt; yellow rounded head (a hat or hair); hands visible at lower centre. 
STYLE: The figures are rendered as assemblages of rounded, cylindrical, tube-like forms — arms, torsos, and skirts all treated as smooth geometric volumes with strong tonal modelling (highlights and shadows). No sharp edges — all forms are curved and rolling. The surfaces have a smooth, almost metallic sheen — oil paint applied with controlled modelling. 
BACKGROUND: Densely packed cylindrical/tube forms in warm orange, golden-yellow, and green — the rye sheaves or harvest crop filling the entire background and ground plane. The background forms are the same cylindrical vocabulary as the figures — foreground and background merge into a single field of rolling tubular forms. 
PALETTE: Deep warm orange-amber (dominant, background and figure), red (left figure skirt and head), blue (centre figure), mauve/purple (right figure top), teal-green (right figure skirt and background areas), white (highlights), yellow-gold (harvest crop and right head). 
COMPOSITION: Near-square canvas completely filled — no empty space or sky visible. The three figures create a circular/rotating composition, all bending inward toward the centre. Strongly influenced by Léger's tubism and Gleizes/Metzinger Cubism, but applied to Ukrainian peasant agricultural subject matter. 
SUBJECT NOTE: Rye harvesting was the primary agricultural activity in the Ukrainian steppe communities where Malevich grew up — the subject is autobiographically as well as culturally significant. 19 library documents.

records.Image: Notes:
Oil on canvas, 80 × 95 cm. Landscape format (wider than tall). Framed (narrow dark frame visible at edges). Currently on view at Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. A large Cubo-Futurist composition depicting a peasant girl's head dissolved into intersecting geometric planes. 
COMPOSITION: The canvas is filled edge-to-edge with a dense, interlocking arrangement of angular planes and facets — no empty space, no clear background. A central pyramidal/conical mass occupies the upper-centre, reading as the girl's head and shoulders: CENTRAL FORM — a large triangular/pyramidal structure of intersecting planes: warm golden-ochre/tan planes (lit surfaces) alternating with deep blue-grey planes (shadowed surfaces). Within the central mass: two dark circular forms (eyes or buttons — ambiguous), one lower-left and one upper-right of centre, rendered as dark grey-blue discs. A vertical cylindrical form (neck/collar) at the lower centre. SURROUNDING PLANES — the composition extends outward in all directions with faceted angular planes: UPPER-RIGHT: a large flat green triangular plane — the most distinctly coloured element, providing a cool contrast to the warm centre. UPPER-LEFT: dark blue-grey angular planes. LOWER areas: warm ochre/amber and dark blue-grey interlocking triangles and wedge forms. 
PALETTE: Warm golden-ochre/tan (dominant lit surfaces), deep blue-grey/navy (dominant shadow surfaces), green (upper-right accent), with subtle dark brown and off-white highlights. The palette is restrained — essentially two dominant tones (warm/cool) with one colour accent. Applied with visible brushwork — short directional strokes following the plane surfaces, creating a slightly textured surface consistent with Divisionist/pointillist influence. 
SIGNATURE: Lower-left — "К.Малевич" in Cyrillic, clearly legible. 
STYLE: This is among the most fully resolved Cubo-Futurist works in the Stedelijk collection — the human figure entirely dissolved into geometric facets, with no legible facial anatomy remaining. The pyramidal central structure and surrounding angular planes recall Picasso's Analytical Cubism of 1910–12 but processed through Malevich's own geometric vocabulary. 29 library documents — reflecting major scholarly attention.

Accession A 7657 (confirmed). 49 linked library documents — the SECOND HIGHEST document count in the entire dataset (after MAL-236, Eight Red Rectangles, with 58 docs), confirming this as one of the most extensively researched works in the collection. Translated title: "Lady at a Poster Column" (Dutch: Dame bij reclamezuil). Stedelijk classifies as "Other" — anomalous given the work is a major oil-and-collage painting. records.Image: Notes:
Oil on canvas with pasted collage elements, 71 × 64 cm. Portrait format. A densely layered Cubo-Futurist/Alogist composition — the only confirmed oil-and-collage work in the dataset. 
OVERALL STRUCTURE: The canvas is divided into large flat colour zones in the manner of Synthetic Cubism, with a dense collage area occupying the upper-centre. COLOUR ZONES: large cream/pale yellow rectangle (lower-left, approximately 40% of canvas); large pink rectangle (upper-centre-right); pale blue/lavender rectangle (left); blue rectangle (right-centre); dark red/brown triangle (lower-right); large black rectangle (lower-centre-right); pale grey/light blue (upper-left background). 
COLLAGE AREA (upper-centre — the primary focus): A complex assembly of overlapping pasted paper fragments and painted forms: PASTED TEXT ELEMENTS — "THÉVENOT" in black serif type on white ground (horizontal strip, centre); "ЗА КВАРТИРА" in Russian newsprint (horizontal strip, centre-left); a decorative ornamental border strip (gold/brown pattern, horizontal, lower of the two text strips); various additional Cyrillic text fragments (partially legible). LARGE LETTERFORMS — a large Cyrillic "У" (left side, blue/purple, partially painted); a large Cyrillic "В" (right side, black, bold, approximately one-quarter of the canvas height). PHOTOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTS — a small portrait photograph (upper-right, showing a standing figure in dark clothing); a small oval portrait (upper-left area). PAINTED COLLAGE FORMS — a large blue ovoid/egg shape (centre); a circular form with concentric markings; an arrow/chevron form (right-centre, blue); a teapot or vessel silhouette (lower-right of collage area); green geometric forms (upper-left of collage); a grey circular form with crosshatch/target pattern. 
FRAMING: narrow dark frame visible at all four edges. 
KEY TEXTS LEGIBLE: "THÉVENOT" (French commercial text); "ЗА КВАРТИРА" (Russian newsprint); "разошелся без" (Russian: "dispersed/sold out without" — partially legible newsprint fragment, lower-centre of collage); Cyrillic characters У, В, О visible as large letterforms.

records.Image: Notes:
Oil on canvas, 84 × 69.5 cm. Portrait format (taller than wide). A monumental Suprematist cross composition — two overlapping rectangular forms creating a bold, hieratic cross shape against a white ground. 
COMPOSITION: Two large geometric elements: RED VERTICAL — a deep crimson/red rectangle occupying the centre-left to centre-right of the canvas, running full height: upper portion (above the black bar): a tall red rectangle, roughly square, upper-centre; lower portion (below the black bar): a taller red rectangle, narrower, centre; the lower red element is longer than the upper. BLACK HORIZONTAL — a very wide, shallow black rectangle crossing the full canvas width at mid-height, overlapping the red vertical and dividing it into upper and lower sections. The black bar is much wider than it is tall — a broad horizontal band. GROUND: off-white/cream — pure, flat, unworked. 
SURFACE: Both the red and black forms have heavily worked, expressive surfaces — the black bar in particular shows vigorous directional brushwork with visible green undertones emerging through the black (consistent with aged black oil paint). The red areas show textured, layered paint application with visible brushstrokes. The cross structure is frontal, symmetrical, and centrally placed — filling most of the canvas. 
ICONOGRAPHY: The Stedelijk title explicitly uses "hiëratisch" (hieratic/sacred) — acknowledging the religious dimension of the cross motif. The two-colour (red + black) cross on white is the most reduced version of the cross motif in the Stedelijk collection — compare Wit suprematistisch kruis (MAL-239, white-on-grey) and Mystiek suprematisme (MAL-213, red cross). The overlapping black-over-red creates a third implicit zone where the colours meet. 37 library documents. Currently on view.

records.Misattribution Notes: Col 6 — ⚠ Wrong label: Pompidou catalogue explicitly states 'Nationalité russe'. Birth location given as 'Bialystok (Lituanie, Empire Russe)' — geographic framing within Russian Empire erases Ukrainian identity. Exter was born in Białystok but raised, educated and culturally formed in Kyiv (Kiev School of Art). The Pompidou record also references AWARE (which correctly identifies her as Ukrainian-born) yet retains the 'Nationalité russe' label — a direct contradiction within the same institutional ecosystem. Set design for Potemkin's play 'Don Juan and Death', intended for Italian troupe of Tatiana Pavlova — project unrealised. Domaine public. Inv. LUX.851 D. Companion to MoMA EXT-025 (205.1972.8) — same subject, different institution.

records.Misattribution Notes: Col 6 — ⚠ Internal contradiction: The Thyssen catalogue text explicitly states 'Alexandra Exter, a painter of Ukrainian origin' and references 'her beloved Kyiv' — yet the work is placed in Room 43 '20th Century. Abstract Utopias' under the tag '20th Century - European painting. Russian avant-garde', and the room navigation labels it under the Russian avant-garde sequence. This is the clearest case in the dataset of an institution simultaneously acknowledging Ukrainian origin in body text while embedding the work in a Russian avant-garde taxonomic framework. records.Misattribution Notes: Col 6 — STRUCTURAL MISATTRIBUTION (not field-level): Yale correctly labels Kakabadzé 'Georgian, 1889–1952' and Culture field states 'Georgian'. However the work entered Yale as part of the Société Anonyme Collection (Gift of Collection Société Anonyme, 1941) — a collection historically framed in scholarship and publications as 'Russian and Eastern European avant-garde'. The key bibliographic reference cited in this record — Robert L. Herbert et al., The Société Anonyme and the Dreier Bequest at Yale University: A Catalogue Raisonné (Yale University Press, 1984) — frames the entire collection within a Russian/Soviet avant-garde narrative. Provenance: Katherine S. Dreier purchase from the artist, Paris, 1927 — acquired directly from Kakabadze before his return to Soviet-controlled Georgia. The structural absorption of this Georgian artist into the Société Anonyme 'Russian avant-garde' canon is the misattribution, not the individual field label. No Copyright — United States.

records.Image: Notes: Watercolour on paper, 23.5 × 18.2 cm (9 1/4 × 7 3/16 in.). White ground. An abstract biomorphic composition — organic, freely flowing forms. PALETTE: deep teal/blue-green (dominant), cobalt blue (upper), violet/purple-magenta (two large forms centre), black (two forms — one rectangular within the purple, one amoeboid lower-centre). FORMS: Upper area — large cobalt blue cloud-like form and smaller blue blobs. Centre-left — large violet/magenta irregular form with a black rectangular void/window inside, and two small blue dots; Centre-right — smaller violet/magenta pear/kidney form. Throughout — multiple teal brush-stroke forms: curved commas, elongated blobs, irregular patches covering the lower half and edges. Two large teal rounded forms upper-left. Signature lower right: "D. Kakabadze. 1921." Gift of Collection Société Anonyme. Katherine S. Dreier purchase from the artist, Paris, 1927. Previously incorrectly duplicated as KAK-003 image — now corrected.

records.Title: Z (The Speared Fish)
records.Medium: Painted wood with metal and glass
records.Holding Institution: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven, Connecticut
records.Misattribution Notes: Col 6 — STRUCTURAL MISATTRIBUTION (not field-level): Yale correctly labels 'Georgian, 1889–1952' and Culture: 'Georgian'. CENTREPIECE RECORD — the most significant single work in the Kakabadze dataset. This is Kakabadze's only surviving sculpture. Exhibited at Salon des Indépendants 1926 — the same year Dreier purchased it for the Société Anonyme. Immediately became an icon of the Société Anonyme Collection, appearing on the cover of numerous pamphlets and publications — yet framed consistently within 'Russian and Eastern European avant-garde' Société Anonyme narrative, not Georgian. Catalogue body text explicitly states: 'In 1919 the Georgian government granted David Kakabadzé [...] a stipend to study in Paris' and 'in 1928 Kakabadzé returned to Georgia, where the Russian government had outlawed abstract art' — the text correctly distinguishes between the Georgian artist and the Russian government that suppressed him. This is the sharpest Yale record for the structural misattribution argument: the institution correctly knows he is Georgian and that the Russian government suppressed him, yet the Société Anonyme publication record consistently framed him as part of 'Russian avant-garde'. Copyright: David Kakabadze/David Kakabadze Foundation (In Copyright).

records.Title: La Grande ville (The Great City)
records.Holding Institution: Centre Pompidou, Musée National d'Art Moderne, Paris
records.Misattribution Notes: Col 6 — ⚠ Wrong label (imperial framing): Pompidou labels Pagava 'Vera Pagava (1907, Empire Russe - 1988, France)'. 'Empire Russe' is technically accurate as a birthplace fact — Georgia was part of the Russian Empire — but as a catalogue label it functions as misattribution because: (1) it subsumes her Georgian identity into a Russian imperial frame, perpetuating the same erasure the empire itself performed; (2) Georgia was an occupied nation with a distinct language, culture and artistic tradition; (3) Pagava's family fled before Soviet annexation (1921) precisely to preserve Georgian identity; (4) Pagava explicitly identified as Georgian throughout her life, living in the Georgian émigré community, never taking French citizenship. Compare: a Belgian artist under German occupation would not be catalogued as 'German Empire'. Donated by Mme Elisso Tarassachvili, 2016 — the Tarassachvili family were central figures in the Georgian Paris émigré community (Galerie Darial). Exhibited in 'Elles font l'abstraction' (Pompidou 2021) and 'Women in Abstraction' (Shanghai 2023).
